mech-w1-q1.question: A 50 N force acts at 30° above the +x axis (anticlockwise). What are its x and y components?
mech-w1-q1.explanation: Fx = 50 cos30° = 43.3 N and Fy = 50 sin30° = 25.0 N. The most common trap is swapping sin and cos (25.0, 43.3), which would be right only if the angle were measured from the y-axis. 57.7 N comes from dividing 50 by cos30°.

mech-w1-q2.question: A couple acts on a plate: two parallel, opposite 40 N forces whose lines of action are 0.25 m apart. Point P on the plate is 2 m away from the couple. What is the moment of the couple about P?
options: 0, because the net force is zero
mech-w1-q2.explanation: The moment of a couple = F·d = 40 × 0.25 = 10 N·m, and it is the same about every point, so it is 10 N·m about P too. 80 N·m comes from wrongly multiplying by the 2 m distance. A zero net force does not mean a zero moment — that is the whole point of a couple.

mech-w1-q3.question: A force F = (3i + 4j) N acts at the point r = (2i + 1j) m. What is its moment about the origin O? (CCW positive)
mech-w1-q3.explanation: M_O = x·Fy − y·Fx = 2·4 − 1·3 = 8 − 3 = 5 N·m. It is positive, so CCW. 11 N·m comes from adding the two terms (forgetting the minus sign). 11.2 N·m = |r|·|F| = √5 × 5, which would only be right if r and F were perpendicular.

mech-w1-q4.question: Two forces act at a point: F1 = 100 N along the +x axis (0°), and F2 = 60 N at 120° from the +x axis. What is the magnitude of the resultant?
mech-w1-q4.explanation: Rx = 100 + 60 cos120° = 100 − 30 = 70 N, Ry = 60 sin120° = 52.0 N. |R| = √(70² + 52.0²) = 87.2 N. 140 N comes from using cos60° instead of cos120° (the angle between the forces is 120°, not 60°). 116.6 N assumes they are perpendicular, and 160 N is the scalar sum.

mech-w1-q5.question: A horizontal bar AB is 0.8 m long. A 500 N vertical force acts downward at end B. Replace this force by an equivalent force-couple system at point A.
options: 500 N down at A and a 200 N·m clockwise couple
500 N down at A and a 400 N·m counter-clockwise couple
Only 500 N down at A, no couple
500 N down at A and a 400 N·m clockwise couple
mech-w1-q5.explanation: Move the force to A and add a couple equal to the moment of the force at B about A = 500 × 0.8 = 400 N·m. B is to the right of A and the force points down, so it turns the bar clockwise. Getting the direction wrong (CCW) is the most common trap; dropping the couple is also wrong, because the turning effect would then disappear.

mech-w1-q6.question: A 6 m horizontal beam has A at x = 0. Loads: 8 kN down at x = 1 m, 4 kN down at x = 4 m, and a 12 kN·m clockwise couple at x = 5 m. How far from A is the line of action of the single resultant force of this system?
mech-w1-q6.explanation: R = 8 + 4 = 12 kN down. Moment about A (CCW +): −8·1 − 4·4 − 12 = −36 kN·m. A single 12 kN downward force at distance x: −12x = −36, x = 3 m. Ignoring the couple gives −24/12 = 2 m — a couple does not change the resultant force but it does shift its location. Taking the couple with the wrong sign gives 1 m.

mech-w1-q7.question: An 80 N force acts at 60° above the +x axis (anticlockwise). What is its y-component Fy?
mech-w1-q7.explanation: Fy = 80 sin60° = 69.3 N. 40.0 N is 80 cos60° — that is the x-component, not y (the sin/cos swap trap). 92.4 N comes from dividing 80 by sin60°; no component can be larger than the whole force, and 80.0 N is the whole force itself.

mech-w1-q8.question: Riya applies a 120 N force perpendicular to a spanner handle, 0.25 m from the centre of the nut. What is the moment on the nut?
mech-w1-q8.explanation: M = F·d = 120 × 0.25 = 30 N·m; the force is perpendicular to the handle, so the full 0.25 m is the perpendicular distance. 480 N·m comes from dividing the force by the distance (120/0.25). 15 N·m has a ½ that does not belong, and 120 N·m is just the force, not a moment.

mech-w1-q9.question: A 15 N·m couple acts on a rigid plate. If this couple is moved (with the same sense) to another place on the plate, what happens to its effect on the plate?
options: A new couple of shift distance × 15 must be added
The effect becomes zero, because the net force is zero
The moment grows with the shift distance
The effect stays the same; a couple is a free vector
mech-w1-q9.explanation: The moment of a couple is the same about every point, so it can be moved anywhere on a rigid body without changing its effect. You add a new couple only when you move a force, not a couple — that is the trap. A zero net force does not remove the turning effect.

mech-w1-q10.question: A force F = 50 N acts at point P (3 m, 2 m) in a direction 60° above the +x axis. What is its moment about the origin O? (CCW positive)
mech-w1-q10.explanation: Fx = 50 cos60° = 25 N, Fy = 50 sin60° = 43.3 N. M_O = x·Fy − y·Fx = 3·43.3 − 2·25 = 129.9 − 50 = 79.9 N·m; it is positive, so CCW. 179.9 N·m comes from forgetting the minus sign and adding the two terms. 180.3 N·m = |r|·|F| = √13 × 50, which is right only if r and F were perpendicular. The clockwise option is a misread sign.

mech-w1-q11.question: Three forces act at a point: F1 = 40 N (+x direction), F2 = 30 N (+y direction) and F3 = 20 N (−x direction). What is the magnitude of the resultant?
mech-w1-q11.explanation: Rx = 40 − 20 = 20 N, Ry = 30 N, so |R| = √(20² + 30²) = 36.1 N. 90.0 N is the scalar sum (ignoring directions). 67.1 N comes from adding F3 in +x as well (Rx = 60). 50.0 N is the resultant of just 40 and 30, forgetting F3.

mech-w1-q12.question: A 6 m horizontal beam has A at x = 0. Loads: 6 kN down at x = 2 m, 4 kN up at x = 5 m, 10 kN down at x = 6 m, and an 8 kN·m counter-clockwise couple. How far from A is the line of action of this system's single resultant force? (Up positive, CCW positive)
mech-w1-q12.explanation: R = −6 + 4 − 10 = −12 kN (12 kN down). M_A = 2(−6) + 5(4) + 6(−10) + 8 = −12 + 20 − 60 + 8 = −44 kN·m. Single force: −12x = −44, so x = 3.67 m. 4.33 m comes from ignoring the couple (−52/−12), and 5.00 m from reversing the couple's sign (−60/−12). 4.20 m comes from treating the 4 kN upward force as downward too (−84/−20).

mech-w1-q13.question: A force F = (4j + 3k) N acts at the point r = (2i + 1j) m. What is the moment of F about the axis through the origin along the unit vector λ = (0.6i + 0.8j)?
mech-w1-q13.explanation: First M_O = r × F = (1·3 − 0·4)i − (2·3 − 0·0)j + (2·4 − 1·0)k = (3i − 6j + 8k) N·m. The moment about the axis = λ · M_O = 0.6·3 + 0.8·(−6) = 1.8 − 4.8 = −3.0 N·m (minus = opposite to the sense of λ). +6.6 N·m comes from dropping the minus on the j-component. 10.4 N·m = |M_O| = √109, the magnitude of the whole moment, not its component along the axis. +3.0 N·m comes from the reversed order (F × r).

mech-w1-q14.question: On a bracket, point B is at (0.4 m, 0.3 m) from point A (x right, y up). A 300 N force acts at B, pointing to the right at 60° below the horizontal. Replace this force by an equivalent force-couple system at A. What is the couple at A?
mech-w1-q14.explanation: Fx = 300 cos60° = 150 N, Fy = −300 sin60° = −259.8 N. M_A = x·Fy − y·Fx = 0.4(−259.8) − 0.3(150) = −103.9 − 45 = −148.9 N·m, i.e. 148.9 N·m clockwise; the force at A stays the same 300 N. 58.9 N·m comes from reversing the sign of the y·Fx term. 150.0 N·m = |r|·|F| = 0.5 × 300, i.e. the full distance instead of the perpendicular distance. CCW is a misread sign.

mech-w1-q15.question: Two couples act on a plate: the first from two 50 N forces whose lines are 0.4 m apart (CCW), the second from two 30 N forces whose lines are 0.5 m apart (clockwise). Their net effect is to be given by a couple of two vertical forces whose lines are 0.25 m apart. How large must each force be?
mech-w1-q15.explanation: Couples are free vectors, so just add them: 50 × 0.4 = 20 N·m CCW and 30 × 0.5 = 15 N·m clockwise, net = 5 N·m CCW. New couple: F × 0.25 = 5, so F = 20 N (in the CCW sense). 140 N comes from treating both couples as the same sense (35/0.25). 1.25 N comes from multiplying instead of dividing (5 × 0.25), and 35 N from taking the sum of moments as the force.

mech-w2-q1.question: In a 2D problem, how many unknown reaction components does a fixed (built-in) support provide?
mech-w2-q1.explanation: A fixed support prevents translation (Rx, Ry) and rotation (a reaction moment M), so 3 unknowns. 2 is the answer for a pin — the moment is exactly the difference between a fixed support and a pin. 1 is for a roller.

mech-w2-q2.question: A 5 kg lamp hangs from two cables. The cables are symmetric and each makes 30° with the horizontal. What is the tension in each cable? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w2-q2.explanation: Weight = 5 × 9.81 = 49.05 N. Vertical equilibrium: 2T sin30° = 49.05, so T = 49.05 / (2 × 0.5) = 49.1 N. 24.5 N comes from simply splitting the weight in two (ignoring the angle). 28.3 N comes from using cos instead of sin — the angle is given from the horizontal, so the vertical component is T sin30°.

mech-w2-q3.question: Cantilever AB is 3 m long, fixed into a wall at A with B the free end (the beam runs to the right of A). There is a 2 kN downward load at 1 m from A and a 4 kN downward load at B. Neglect the beam's weight. What is the reaction moment at A?
mech-w2-q3.explanation: The loads' moment about A = 2·1 + 4·3 = 14 kN·m clockwise, so the wall must supply 14 kN·m counter-clockwise. Writing the direction of the loads' moment instead is the most common trap. 18 kN·m comes from multiplying the total 6 kN by 3 m, and 6 kN·m from mixing up force and moment.

mech-w2-q4.question: A 200 N block hangs from point C. From C, rope CA runs horizontally to a wall, and a second rope CB runs up to the ceiling at 40° from the vertical. What is the tension in rope CA?
mech-w2-q4.explanation: Joint C: vertical: T_CB cos40° = 200, so T_CB = 261.1 N. Horizontal: T_CA = T_CB sin40° = 200 tan40° = 167.8 N. 238.4 N = 200/tan40°, which comes from treating the angle as measured from the horizontal. 128.6 N and 153.2 N come from multiplying 200 directly by sin or cos.

mech-w2-q5.question: A horizontal beam has pin supports at both ends A and B (two pins, no roller). It carries vertical loads. What is this beam?
mech-w2-q5.explanation: Two pins = 2 + 2 = 4 unknowns, but 2D gives only 3 equations, so the degree of indeterminacy is 4 − 3 = 1. Even with vertical loads, Ax and Bx cannot be found separately; you only get their sum (Ax + Bx = 0). 'Determinate' is the mistake of not counting the reactions.

mech-w2-q6.question: A uniform horizontal bar AB, 2 m long and weighing 200 N, is pinned to a wall at A. From end B a cable runs up to point C on the wall, making 30° with the bar. A 400 N weight hangs from B. What is the horizontal reaction at pin A?
mech-w2-q6.explanation: ΣM_A = 0: T sin30°·2 = 200·1 + 400·2 = 1000, so T = 1000 N. Horizontal: Ax = T cos30° = 866.0 N (pushing out from the wall). 692.8 N comes from forgetting the bar's own 200 N weight (T = 800 N). 1000 N is the cable tension, not the reaction, and 500 N is its vertical component.

mech-w2-q7.question: In which direction does a roller support resting on a horizontal surface apply its reaction to a beam?
options: A force and a reaction moment
mech-w2-q7.explanation: A roller can roll back and forth on the surface, so it cannot push along the surface — only perpendicular to it, i.e. 1 unknown. Both components come from a pin, and a force plus a moment from a fixed support. Assuming a parallel (horizontal) force at a roller is the most common FBD mistake.

mech-w2-q8.question: A simply supported beam AB has a 5 m span (pin at A, roller at B). A 20 kN vertical load acts downward 2 m from A. What is the reaction R_B?
mech-w2-q8.explanation: ΣM_A = 0: R_B·5 = 20·2, so R_B = 8 kN, and R_A = 20 − 8 = 12 kN. 12 kN is R_A — the load is nearer A, so A carries more and B less. 10 kN would be right only for a load at midspan. 40 kN is force × distance, forgetting to divide by the span.

mech-w2-q9.question: A straight, weightless link AB is connected by smooth pins at both ends and carries no load in between. What is the direction of the forces on the link?
options: Any direction, depending on the pins
mech-w2-q9.explanation: This is a two-force member: forces at only two points and no moment. ΣM = 0 is possible only if both forces lie along the line joining those two points, and ΣF = 0 makes them equal and opposite. Perpendicular forces would form an unbalanced couple. The weight is neglected, so the gravity reason is wrong too.

mech-w2-q10.question: A 100 N weight hangs from a ring held by two strings: the left string at 30° to the horizontal and the right string at 60° to the horizontal. What is the tension in the right (60°) string?
mech-w2-q10.explanation: Horizontal: T₁ cos30° = T₂ cos60°, so T₁ = 0.577 T₂. Vertical: T₁ sin30° + T₂ sin60° = 100 ⇒ T₂(0.289 + 0.866) = 100, T₂ = 86.6 N (and T₁ = 50.0 N). By Lami too: the strings are 90° apart, so T₂ = 100 sin120°/sin90° = 86.6 N. 50.0 N is the other string's tension. 115.5 N = 100/sin60°, which would hold only if one string carried the whole weight alone.

mech-w2-q11.question: A simply supported beam AB has a 6 m span (pin at A, roller at B). A 20 kN force acts 4 m from A, inclined at 30° to the beam (pointing downward). What is the roller reaction R_B?
mech-w2-q11.explanation: Only the vertical component enters the moment (the horizontal one lies along the beam): 20 sin30° = 10 kN. ΣM_A: R_B·6 = 10·4, R_B = 6.67 kN. 13.33 kN comes from treating the whole 20 kN as vertical. 11.55 kN comes from using the cos30° component (17.32 kN). 3.33 kN is R_A.

mech-w2-q12.question: A cantilever AB, 2 m long, is fixed into a wall at A (the beam runs to the right of A). At the free end B a 5 kN force acts at 30° below the horizontal, pointing right (away from the wall). A 4 kN·m counter-clockwise couple also acts at mid-length. What is the reaction moment at A?
mech-w2-q12.explanation: Components at B: horizontal 4.33 kN (along the beam line, zero moment) and vertical 5 sin30° = 2.5 kN down. Moment of the loads about A: −2.5 × 2 + 4 = −1 kN·m (clockwise), so the wall supplies M_A = 1 kN·m CCW. 5 kN·m comes from forgetting the couple. 6 kN·m comes from using the full 5 kN × 2 m (10 − 4), and 9 kN·m from reversing the couple's sign (5 + 4).

mech-w2-q13.question: A smooth 500 N sphere rests in a V-groove whose two smooth walls are inclined at 30° and 45° to the horizontal. What is the normal reaction from the 30° wall?
mech-w2-q13.explanation: Each wall's reaction is perpendicular to the wall, so N₁ is at 30° to the vertical and N₂ at 45° (on opposite sides). Lami: N₁ and N₂ are 75° apart; the angle opposite N₁ (between N₂ and W) is 135°. N₁ = 500 sin135°/sin75° = 366.0 N, and N₂ = 500 sin150°/sin75° = 258.8 N. 258.8 N swaps the two reactions. 433.0 N = 500 cos30°, the answer for a block on a single incline, not a groove. 250.0 N just halves the weight.

mech-w2-q14.question: A horizontal beam AB, 4 m long, has a pin at A. At B a roller rests on a surface inclined at 30° to the horizontal, so the reaction at B is at 30° to the vertical. A 12 kN vertical load acts downward at midspan. What is the magnitude of the horizontal reaction at pin A?
mech-w2-q14.explanation: Components of R_B: vertical R_B cos30°, horizontal R_B sin30°. ΣM_A: R_B cos30° × 4 = 12 × 2, so R_B = 6/0.866 = 6.93 kN. ΣFx: A_x balances the horizontal component of R_B: R_B sin30° = 3.46 kN. 0 kN comes from assuming the roller reaction is vertical. 6.93 kN is R_B itself. 3.00 kN comes from taking R_B = 6 kN (forgetting cos30°) and halving it.

mech-w2-q15.question: A uniform horizontal beam AB, 3 m long and weighing 600 N, is pinned at A. A vertical cable runs upward from point C, 2 m from A, and a 900 N load hangs from end B. What is the vertical reaction at pin A?
mech-w2-q15.explanation: ΣM_A: T·2 = 600·1.5 + 900·3 = 3600, so T = 1800 N. ΣFy: A_y + 1800 − 600 − 900 = 0, A_y = −300 N, i.e. 300 N downward — the cable is at C and the big load at B, so the beam tends to pivot about C and lift the A end. "300 N upward" comes from not checking the sign. 450 N downward comes from forgetting the beam's weight (T = 1350 N). 1500 N upward comes from ignoring the cable and putting all loads on A.

mech-w3-q1.question: A joint of a truss has no external load or support, and only two members meet there, not in one line (non-collinear). What is true about the forces in these two members?
options: They are equal and opposite, but non-zero
Nothing can be said without the rest of the truss's loads
mech-w3-q1.explanation: Two non-collinear forces can only sum to zero if both are zero — neither has a component that the other could cancel. So this is known without any calculation. 'Equal and opposite' is only possible for collinear members.

mech-w3-q2.question: A plane truss has 6 joints, 9 members and 3 reaction components from its supports (one pin, one roller). What can be said about its determinacy?
options: Statically determinate (if the members are properly arranged)
mech-w3-q2.explanation: m + r = 9 + 3 = 12 and 2j = 2 × 6 = 12. They are equal, so unknowns = equations and the truss is determinate (provided the members are arranged so the shape is stable). The mistake is comparing with j or 3j instead of 2j.

mech-w3-q3.question: Triangular truss: pin at A (0, 0), roller at B (6 m, 0), and a 12 kN vertical downward load at apex C (3 m, 4 m). What is the force in the horizontal member AB?
mech-w3-q3.explanation: Reactions are 6 kN each. AC is 5 m long, so sinθ = 4/5, cosθ = 3/5. Joint A: F_AC·(4/5) + 6 = 0, F_AC = −7.5 kN (C). ΣFx: F_AB + F_AC·(3/5) = 0, F_AB = +4.5 kN, i.e. tension. 7.5 kN compression is the force in AC, not AB. 8.0 kN comes from swapping sin and cos.

mech-w3-q4.question: In the bridge truss below, bottom joints A, B, C, D, E are 3 m apart (A at x = 0, E at x = 12 m). Top joints F, G, H are 3 m directly above B, C, D. Members: AB, BC, CD, DE, FG, GH, AF, HE, FB, GC, HD, FC, HC. Pin at A, roller at E, and 10 kN down at B, C, D. Which member is a zero-force member?
mech-w3-q4.explanation: Joint G has three members: FG and GH are collinear (both horizontal) and GC is vertical, with no load at G. By rule 2, GC = 0. The trap is FB: joint B shows the same pattern (AB, BC collinear + FB), but B carries a 10 kN load, so FB = 10 kN tension, not zero.

mech-w3-q5.question: In the same bridge truss (bottom joints 3 m apart, height 3 m, pin at A, roller at E, 10 kN down at B, C, D), what is the force in top-chord member FG? The section cuts members FG, FC and BC.
mech-w3-q5.explanation: Reactions: Ay = Ey = 15 kN. Take the left part and sum moments about C (x = 6, y = 0) — FC and BC both pass through C. taking clockwise +: 15·6 − 10·3 + F_FG·3 = 0 (F_FG assumed tension: at F it pulls toward G, i.e. to the right, 3 m above C), so F_FG = −20 kN, i.e. 20 kN compression. 30 kN comes from forgetting the 10 kN load at B; 15 kN is the force in bottom chord BC.

mech-w3-q6.question: In the same bridge truss (pin at A, roller at E, 10 kN down at B, C, D, panels 3 m × 3 m), what is the force in diagonal FC?
mech-w3-q6.explanation: Use the same section (FG, FC, BC). FG and BC are horizontal, so vertical equilibrium involves only FC, which runs from F down to C at 45°. ΣFy: 15 − 10 − F_FC sin45° = 0, so F_FC = 5/0.707 = +7.07 kN, tension. 5.0 kN comes from forgetting the 45° angle and giving the whole vertical shear to FC. 21.2 kN is the force in end diagonal AF (and that is compression).

mech-w3-q7.question: What is true about the force in a member of an ideal plane truss?
options: A force along the axis plus a bending moment
Depends on the joint, in any direction
Along the member axis (T or C)
mech-w3-q7.explanation: Truss members are pinned at their ends and loads act only at joints, so every member is a two-force member — the force is only along its axis, tension or compression. A bending moment would appear only if a load acted between the ends, which does not happen in an ideal truss. The shear option is beam thinking.

mech-w3-q8.question: A plane truss has 5 joints, 8 members and 3 reaction components from its supports. What is this truss?
mech-w3-q8.explanation: m + r = 8 + 3 = 11 and 2j = 2 × 5 = 10. 11 > 10, so there is one extra unknown: indeterminate, degree 1. "Determinate" would need m + r = 2j (7 members). "Unstable" is for m + r < 2j — the opposite of this case. Degree 3 has no basis — there is only 11 − 10 = 1 extra unknown.

mech-w3-q9.question: At an unloaded truss joint three members meet: two collinear and a third in a different direction. What is true about the forces in the collinear members?
options: One is in tension, the other must be in compression
They equal the third member's force
mech-w3-q9.explanation: Take ΣF perpendicular to the collinear line: only the third member has a component that way, so it is zero. Then ΣF = 0 along the collinear line makes the two collinear forces equal (both T or both C). "Both zero" confuses this with rule 1 (only two non-collinear members). One T and one C would mean both pull the joint the same way — with the tension convention they come out the same type.

mech-w3-q10.question: Triangular truss: pin at A (0, 0), roller at B (8 m, 0), and an 18 kN vertical load downward at apex C (4 m, 3 m). What is the force in member AC?
mech-w3-q10.explanation: By symmetry A_y = B_y = 9 kN. AC is 5 m long, sinθ = 3/5, cosθ = 4/5. Joint A (assuming AC in tension): F_AC·(3/5) + 9 = 0, F_AC = −15 kN, i.e. compression. 12 kN tension is the force in AB (−F_AC·4/5). 11.25 kN comes from swapping sin and cos (9/0.8), and "15 kN tension" from ignoring the minus sign.

mech-w3-q11.question: In the bridge truss below, the bottom joints are 3 m apart and the height is 3 m. There is a pin at A, a roller at E, and 10 kN acts downward at each of B, C and D. What is the force in bottom member AB?
mech-w3-q11.explanation: By symmetry A_y = 15 kN. At joint A there are only AB (horizontal) and AF (45°). ΣFy: 15 + F_AF sin45° = 0, F_AF = −21.2 kN (C). ΣFx: F_AB + F_AF cos45° = 0, F_AB = +15 kN, i.e. tension. 21.2 kN compression is the force in AF, not AB. 10.6 kN comes from simply multiplying 15 by cos45°. "15 kN compression" is a misread sign — the bottom chord stops the supports spreading apart, so it is in tension.

mech-w3-q12.question: In the bridge truss below (bottom joints 3 m apart, height 3 m, pin at A, roller at E) there is now an 18 kN downward load at joint C only; B and D carry no load. Which members are zero-force members?
options: All three of FB, GC and HD
FB and HD, but not GC
None, because the truss is loaded
mech-w3-q12.explanation: Joint B: AB and BC are collinear, FB is separate, and B now has no load — by rule 2, FB = 0. Likewise at D (CD, DE collinear) HD = 0, and at G (FG, GH collinear) GC = 0. "Only GC" is the answer for the old loading (B and D loaded too) — change the loads and the zero-force members change. A loaded truss does not make every member loaded; the rule is applied joint by joint.

mech-w3-q13.question: In the bridge truss below there is an 18 kN downward load at joint C only (pin at A, roller at E, panels 3 m × 3 m). What is the force in top member FG? The section cuts FG, FC and BC.
mech-w3-q13.explanation: By symmetry A_y = E_y = 9 kN. Take the left part and sum moments about C (FC and BC both pass through C): A_y gives 9 × 6 = 54 kN·m clockwise. FG is 3 m above C, so F_FG × 3 must balance it: |F_FG| = 18 kN, and assuming tension gives a negative sign, i.e. compression (the top chord is squeezed). "18 kN tension" is a misread sign. 9 kN comes from using 3 m instead of 6 m as the arm of A_y, and 36 kN from putting the whole 18 kN on one support.

mech-w3-q14.question: In a wall-mounted truss, joints A (0, 0) and B (0, 2 m) are both pinned to the wall. The tip C is at (3 m, 0), and the only members are AC (horizontal) and BC (inclined). A 12 kN vertical load acts downward at C. What is the force in member BC?
mech-w3-q14.explanation: Joint C has only two members, so the reactions are not even needed. BC is √(3² + 2²) = 3.606 m long. ΣFy at C: F_BC·(2/3.606) − 12 = 0, F_BC = +21.6 kN, i.e. tension (BC pulls the tip up and toward the wall). ΣFx: F_AC = −F_BC·(3/3.606) = −18.0 kN, so AC is in compression — 18.0 kN is its answer, not BC's. 14.4 kN comes from using 3/3.606 for the vertical component (12 × 3.606/3). "Compression" is the reversed sign.

mech-w3-q15.question: In the bridge truss below there is a 20 kN downward load at joint B only (pin at A, roller at E, bottom joints 3 m apart, height 3 m). What is the force in top member GH?
mech-w3-q15.explanation: Reactions: E_y·12 = 20·3, so E_y = 5 kN and A_y = 15 kN. Cut GH, HC and CD and take the right part (only E_y = 5 kN acts on it, no load). Moments about C: E_y has a 6 m arm, giving 5 × 6 = 30 kN·m, balanced by GH (3 m above C): |F_GH| = 30/3 = 10 kN, compression. 30 kN compression comes from taking the left part and forgetting the 20 kN load at B (15 × 6/3). 5 kN comes from using 3 m instead of 6 m as the arm of E_y.

mech-w4-q1.question: A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a 20 kN point load exactly at midspan. What is the maximum bending moment?
mech-w4-q1.explanation: Both reactions are 10 kN. At midspan M = 10 × 3 = 30 kN·m, i.e. PL/4 = 20 × 6/4. 60 kN·m comes from multiplying the full 20 kN load, instead of the 10 kN reaction, by the half span (3 m). 15 kN·m comes from a UDL-style formula (PL/8).

mech-w4-q2.question: A 2 m cantilever carries a 3 kN/m UDL over its whole length. What is the magnitude of the bending moment at the fixed end?
mech-w4-q2.explanation: Total load = 3 × 2 = 6 kN, acting 1 m (at the middle) from the fixed end. |M| = 6 × 1 = 6 kN·m = wL²/2. 12 kN·m comes from placing the load at the free end (6 × 2). 1.5 kN·m is the simply supported wL²/8, which does not apply to a cantilever.

mech-w4-q3.question: Simply supported beam AB, span 6 m, carries a triangular load that rises from 0 at A to 6 kN/m at B. What is the reaction R_A?
mech-w4-q3.explanation: Total load = ½ × 6 × 6 = 18 kN, with its centroid 6/3 = 2 m from the big end (B), i.e. 4 m from A. ΣM_A: R_B·6 = 18·4, R_B = 12 kN, so R_A = 6 kN. 9 kN comes from placing the resultant at midspan. 12 kN is R_B — the load is heavier towards B, so B carries more.

mech-w4-q4.question: Overhanging beam: pin at A (x = 0), roller at B (x = 4 m), and the beam extends to x = 6 m (point C). There is a 10 kN downward load at C and no other load. What is the reaction at A?
mech-w4-q4.explanation: ΣM_A: R_B·4 = 10·6, R_B = 15 kN up. ΣFy: R_A + 15 − 10 = 0, R_A = −5 kN, i.e. 5 kN downward. The overhang load tips the beam about B like a see-saw and end A wants to lift, so A must pull down. '5 kN upward' comes from not checking the sign.

mech-w4-q5.question: A simply supported beam of span 10 m carries a 30 kN point load 4 m from A. What is the bending moment directly under the load?
mech-w4-q5.explanation: R_A = 30 × 6/10 = 18 kN, R_B = 30 × 4/10 = 12 kN. Under the load M = R_A × 4 = 72 kN·m (from the right side, 12 × 6 = 72 ✓). 75 kN·m is PL/4, which is only for a central load. 48 kN·m comes from multiplying the wrong reaction (12 kN) by 4 m.

mech-w4-q6.question: A simply supported beam of span 8 m carries a 6 kN/m UDL only on its left half (from x = 0 to 4 m). What is the maximum bending moment?
mech-w4-q6.explanation: Load = 24 kN at x = 2 m. R_B = 24·2/8 = 6 kN, R_A = 18 kN. V = 18 − 6x = 0 at x = 3 m. M(3) = 18·3 − 6·3²/2 = 54 − 27 = 27 kN·m. 24 kN·m is the midspan (x = 4) moment — the maximum is where V = 0, not at the middle. 48 kN·m comes from treating it as a full-span UDL with wL²/8.

mech-w4-q7.question: A 3 m cantilever carries a 5 kN point load at its free end. What is the magnitude of the bending moment at the fixed end?
mech-w4-q7.explanation: The free-end load acts with the full length as its arm: |M| = PL = 5 × 3 = 15 kN·m. 7.5 kN·m comes from placing the load at mid-length. 3.75 kN·m is PL/4 for a simply supported beam, which does not apply to a cantilever. 5 kN·m just writes the force as a moment.

mech-w4-q8.question: A beam carries a 2 kN/m UDL over its full 5 m length. To find the reactions, which equivalent point load replaces it?
mech-w4-q8.explanation: The resultant of a UDL = area of the load diagram = 2 × 5 = 10 kN, and a rectangle's centroid is at its middle, i.e. at 2.5 m. 5/3 m (L/3) is the rule for a triangular load, not a UDL. 2 kN is only the intensity (kN/m), not a force. Putting it at an end gives wrong moments.

mech-w4-q9.question: A simply supported beam with an 8 m span carries a 4 kN/m UDL over the whole span. What is the maximum bending moment?
mech-w4-q9.explanation: M_max = wL²/8 = 4 × 64/8 = 32 kN·m, at midspan. 128 kN·m is the cantilever result wL²/2. 64 kN·m comes from treating the total load (32 kN) as a central point load and using PL/4 — that formula is for a point load only. 16 kN·m just writes the reaction (16 kN) as a moment.

mech-w4-q10.question: A simply supported beam AB has a 6 m span. An 18 kN point load acts downward 2 m from A. What is the shear force V at x = 4 m? (V = sum of upward forces on the part left of the section)
mech-w4-q10.explanation: R_A = 18 × 4/6 = 12 kN, R_B = 6 kN. The part left of x = 4 m has R_A = 12 up and 18 down: V = 12 − 18 = −6 kN. +6 kN comes from reversing the sign convention (counting the right part's forces as if they were on the left). +12 kN is the shear before the load (x < 2 m). −18 kN comes from forgetting the reaction and taking only the load.

mech-w4-q11.question: A 3 m cantilever carries a triangular load that is 0 at the free end and 6 kN/m at the fixed end. What is the magnitude of the bending moment at the fixed end?
mech-w4-q11.explanation: Total load = ½ × 6 × 3 = 9 kN, with its centroid L/3 = 1 m from the big end (the fixed end). |M| = 9 × 1 = 9 kN·m. 18 kN·m comes from putting the centroid L/3 from the small end (i.e. 2 m from the fixed end). 13.5 kN·m comes from placing the resultant at mid-length, and 27 kN·m from using the UDL result wL²/2.

mech-w4-q12.question: Overhanging beam: pin at A (x = 0), roller at B (x = 6 m), and the beam extends to x = 8 m. A 3 kN/m UDL acts over the full 8 m. What is the maximum sagging (positive) bending moment between A and B?
mech-w4-q12.explanation: Total 24 kN, at x = 4 m. ΣM_A: R_B·6 = 24·4, R_B = 16 kN, R_A = 8 kN. In AB, V = 8 − 3x = 0 at x = 2.67 m. M = 8(2.67) − 1.5(2.67)² = 21.33 − 10.67 = 10.7 kN·m. 13.5 kN·m is just wL²/8 for the 6 m span — the overhang load causes hogging at B and reduces the sagging. 24.0 kN·m treats the whole 8 m as simply supported, and 6.0 kN·m is the hogging moment at B (3 × 2 × 1), not sagging.

mech-w4-q13.question: A simply supported beam has a 9 m span. Loads of 15 kN at 3 m and 6 kN at 6 m from A act downward. What is the maximum bending moment?
mech-w4-q13.explanation: ΣM_A: R_B·9 = 15·3 + 6·6 = 81, R_B = 9 kN, R_A = 12 kN. M(3) = 12 × 3 = 36 kN·m, M(6) = 9 × 3 = 27 kN·m. V jumps from +12 to −3 at x = 3 m, so the maximum is there: 36 kN·m. 27 kN·m is the moment under the second load. 47.3 kN·m comes from treating both loads as one 21 kN central load with PL/4. 45 kN·m multiplies the load (15 × 3) instead of the reaction.

mech-w4-q14.question: A cantilever AB, 4 m long, is fixed at A. It carries a 2 kN/m UDL over its full length and a 5 kN point load at the free end B. What is the magnitude of the bending moment at mid-length (2 m from A)?
mech-w4-q14.explanation: Use the FBD of the part right of the section (the free part), so no reactions are needed: the UDL on it is 2 × 2 = 4 kN at 1 m from the section, plus 5 kN at 2 m. |M| = 4 × 1 + 5 × 2 = 14 kN·m (hogging). 36 kN·m is the fixed-end moment (16 + 20), not the mid-length one. 10 kN·m comes from forgetting the UDL, and 18 kN·m from wrongly placing that part's UDL resultant at the free end (4 × 2 + 10).

mech-w4-q15.question: A simply supported beam AB with a 6 m span carries a triangular load rising from 0 at A to 6 kN/m at B (R_A = 6 kN, R_B = 12 kN). What is the maximum bending moment?
mech-w4-q15.explanation: At distance x from A the intensity is w = x kN/m (6 kN/m ÷ 6 m). The load on the left part = x²/2, with its centroid x/3 from the section. V = 6 − x²/2 = 0 ⇒ x = √12 = 3.46 m. M = 6x − (x²/2)(x/3) = 20.78 − 6.93 = 13.9 kN·m. 13.5 kN·m is the moment at midspan (x = 3 m) — the maximum is not at the middle but where V = 0. 27.0 kN·m is the UDL result wL²/8. 20.8 kN·m comes from forgetting to subtract the load's moment (x³/6).

mech-w5-q1.question: A portion of a beam carries a uniformly distributed load (w constant). What are the shapes of the SFD and BMD in that portion?
mech-w5-q1.explanation: dV/dx = −w is constant, so V is linear (degree 1). dM/dx = V is linear, so M is degree 2, a parabola. 'V constant, M linear' is a portion with no load. Each integration raises the degree by one — remember that pattern.

mech-w5-q2.question: A 10 kg block rests on a horizontal floor with μs = 0.4. What horizontal force is needed to just start moving it? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w5-q2.explanation: N = mg = 10 × 9.81 = 98.1 N. At impending motion F = μs·N = 0.4 × 98.1 = 39.2 N. 4 N comes from treating the mass as the weight and forgetting g (0.4 × 10). 98.1 N is the weight, not the friction.

mech-w5-q3.question: In a simply supported beam of span 6 m, the shear is V(x) = 12 − 4x kN (x in metres, 0 ≤ x ≤ 6) and M(0) = 0. What is the maximum bending moment?
mech-w5-q3.explanation: M(x) = ∫V dx = 12x − 2x². V = 0 at x = 3 m, so M_max = 12·3 − 2·9 = 36 − 18 = 18 kN·m. This is the area of the SFD triangle from 0 to 3 m: ½ × 3 × 12 = 18. 36 kN·m comes from dropping the −2x² term (12 × 3). 12 kN·m is V(0), not a moment.

mech-w5-q4.question: The coefficient of static friction between a block and an incline is μs = 0.3. What is the maximum incline angle at which the block stays at rest without sliding?
mech-w5-q4.explanation: At the start of slipping, mg sinθ = μs·mg cosθ, so tanθ = μs = 0.3, θ = tan⁻¹(0.3) = 16.7°. 17.5° comes from sin⁻¹(0.3) — the wrong function. 72.5° is cos⁻¹(0.3). The mass cancels, so the answer does not depend on it.

mech-w5-q5.question: A beam carries a 10 kN·m clockwise couple at x = 3 m (and no point force there). Using this course's sign convention (M = clockwise moment of the left-side forces, sagging +), what happens in the diagrams at x = 3 m?
options: V jumps by 10 kN, M is continuous
M jumps up by 10 kN·m, V is unaffected
Both V and M jump by 10
Nothing; a couple only affects the reactions
mech-w5-q5.explanation: A couple has no net force, so V stays continuous. For a section just to the right of the couple, the couple is on the left part and adds +10 kN·m (clockwise) to M — so the BMD steps up by 10 kN·m. Showing a jump in the SFD is the most common mistake; SFD jumps come only from point forces.

mech-w5-q6.question: A uniform ladder of weight 200 N leans against a smooth (frictionless) vertical wall with its lower end on a rough horizontal floor. The ladder makes 60° with the floor. What minimum μs at the floor prevents slipping?
mech-w5-q6.explanation: Let the length be L. The smooth wall gives only a horizontal N_w. Moments about the foot: N_w·L sin60° = 200·(L/2) cos60°, so N_w = 200/(2 tan60°) = 57.7 N. Floor: N = 200 N, friction F = N_w = 57.7 N. μs ≥ 57.7/200 = 0.289. 0.577 (= 1/tan60°) comes from putting the weight at the top end instead of the centre, i.e. dropping the half in L/2.

mech-w5-q7.question: By the load–shear relation, what is the slope dV/dx of the SFD at a point on a beam equal to? (w = downward load intensity)
options: The bending moment M at that point
The shear V at that point
mech-w5-q7.explanation: ΣFy on a small element gives dV/dx = −w: a downward load reduces the shear, hence the minus. "+w" is the forgotten-sign mistake. The "V" relation is for the slope of the BMD (dM/dx = V), not the SFD, and M has no direct link to the SFD slope.

mech-w5-q8.question: A 20 kg block slides on a horizontal floor with μk = 0.25. What is the kinetic friction force on it? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w5-q8.explanation: N = mg = 20 × 9.81 = 196.2 N, F = μk·N = 0.25 × 196.2 = 49.1 N. 5.0 N comes from forgetting g and using the mass as N (0.25 × 20). 196.2 N is the normal reaction, not the friction. 24.5 N has an extra ½ that does not belong.

mech-w5-q9.question: A 10 kg block rests on a horizontal floor with μs = 0.5. Arjun pushes it with a 20 N horizontal force but it does not move. What friction force does the floor exert on the block? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w5-q9.explanation: The block is in equilibrium, so ΣFx = 0: friction = applied force = 20 N. μs·N = 0.5 × 98.1 = 49.1 N is only the maximum possible static friction — it is reached only when the block is about to move. 98.1 N is the normal reaction. 0 N is wrong, because without friction the 20 N would accelerate the block.

mech-w5-q10.question: The SFD of a beam: V = +8 kN from x = 0 to 3 m, and V = −4 kN from x = 3 m to 9 m. M(0) = 0. What is the bending moment at x = 5 m?
mech-w5-q10.explanation: ΔM = area of the SFD. M(3) = 8 × 3 = 24 kN·m. M(5) = 24 + (−4)(2) = 16 kN·m (check: M(9) = 24 − 4 × 6 = 0). 24 kN·m is the (maximum) moment at x = 3 m. 32 kN·m comes from adding the negative area too (dropping its sign). 8 kN·m is only the 3–5 m area, forgetting the earlier 24.

mech-w5-q11.question: A 5 kg block sits on a 30° incline with μs = 0.3. What minimum force parallel to the incline (pointing up the slope) keeps it from sliding down? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w5-q11.explanation: tan30° = 0.577 > 0.3, so without a force the block would slide. It tends to slide down, so friction acts up: P + μs·mg cos30° = mg sin30°. P = 49.05(0.5 − 0.3 × 0.866) = 49.05 × 0.240 = 11.8 N. 37.3 N is the force to start pushing it up (friction reversed). 24.5 N comes from forgetting friction, and 12.7 N is the maximum friction (μs·mg cos30°) itself.

mech-w5-q12.question: A 20 kg crate rests on a horizontal floor with μs = 0.4. A rope pulls it at 30° above the horizontal. What rope tension is needed just to start the crate moving? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w5-q12.explanation: The rope's upward component reduces N: N = 196.2 − T sin30°. Impending motion: T cos30° = 0.4(196.2 − 0.5T) ⇒ T(0.866 + 0.2) = 78.48, T = 73.6 N. 78.5 N is the answer for a horizontal pull (μs·mg). 90.6 N comes from dividing that 78.5 by cos30°, ignoring the change in N. 117.8 N comes from adding T sin30° to N, as if the rope pressed the crate down.

mech-w5-q13.question: A uniform 5 m ladder (weight 200 N) leans against a smooth vertical wall, making 60° with the floor. A 600 N man stands 3 m up the ladder (measured along it) from the bottom end. What minimum μs at the floor stops the ladder slipping?
mech-w5-q13.explanation: Moments about the floor end (the smooth wall gives only a horizontal N_w): N_w × 5 sin60° = 200 × 2.5 cos60° + 600 × 3 cos60° = 250 + 900 = 1150, so N_w = 265.6 N. Floor: N = 200 + 600 = 800 N, and friction F = N_w. μs ≥ 265.6/800 = 0.332. 0.289 is the ladder-only answer, ignoring the man. 0.505 comes from putting the man at the top (5 m). 1.33 comes from using only the ladder's weight (200 N) for N.

mech-w5-q14.question: A simply supported beam AB has a 6 m span (pin at A, roller at B). The only load is a 12 kN·m clockwise couple at x = 2 m. What is the magnitude of the maximum bending moment in the beam, and where is it?
options: 8 kN·m, just right of the couple
4 kN·m, just left of the couple
12 kN·m, exactly at the couple point
mech-w5-q14.explanation: ΣM_A: R_B·6 − 12 = 0, R_B = 2 kN up, R_A = 2 kN down. V = −2 kN along the whole beam (a couple does not change V). Just left of x = 2: M = −2 × 2 = −4 kN·m. A clockwise couple makes M step up by +12, so just right M = +8 kN·m, then it falls linearly to 0 at B (8 − 2 × 4 = 0 ✓). |M|max = 8 kN·m. 4 kN·m is the value on the left side, which is smaller. 12 kN·m is the size of the step, not the maximum moment. 6 kN·m comes from treating the couple like a central point load.

mech-w5-q15.question: Block A (4 kg) rests on block B (6 kg). A is tied to a wall by a horizontal string, so it cannot move. μs = 0.3 between A and B, and μs = 0.2 between B and the floor. What horizontal force P on B is needed just to start B moving? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w5-q15.explanation: Friction on top of B (from A): 0.3 × 4 × 9.81 = 11.8 N. Under B the floor normal = (4 + 6) × 9.81 = 98.1 N, so friction 0.2 × 98.1 = 19.6 N. Both oppose B's motion, so P = 11.8 + 19.6 = 31.4 N. 19.6 N comes from forgetting the A–B friction. 23.5 N comes from taking the floor normal from B's weight alone (0.2 × 58.9 = 11.8). 41.2 N comes from using 0.3 at the floor too (29.4 + 11.8).

mech-w6-q1.question: A spring with k = 400 N/m is compressed 0.05 m from its natural length. How much elastic energy is stored in it?
mech-w6-q1.explanation: Ve = ½kx² = ½ × 400 × 0.05² = 0.5 J. 1.0 J comes from forgetting the ½. 20 and 10 are the force (kx = 20 N) and half of it, not energies.

mech-w6-q2.question: A 3 kg box is lifted 2 m vertically. How much work does gravity (the box's weight) do during this? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
options: 0, because the box goes from rest to rest
mech-w6-q2.explanation: The weight acts down and the displacement is up, so U = −mgΔh = −3 × 9.81 × 2 = −58.9 J. +58.9 J is the work done by the lifter (you), not by gravity. The net work may be zero, but gravity's work alone is not.

mech-w6-q3.question: A spring with k = 500 N/m is pulled from a stretch of 0.1 m to a stretch of 0.3 m. How much work is needed to stretch it over this range?
mech-w6-q3.explanation: U = ½k(x₂² − x₁²) = ½ × 500 × (0.09 − 0.01) = 250 × 0.08 = 20 J. 10 J comes from ½k(Δx)² = ½ × 500 × 0.2², which is wrong because the spring was already stretched. 22.5 J is just the final energy, without subtracting the initial 2.5 J.

mech-w6-q4.question: A ball is released from rest at a height of 5 m on a frictionless track. What is its speed when it reaches a point at a height of 1.8 m? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w6-q4.explanation: Energy conservation: ½v² = g(5 − 1.8) = 9.81 × 3.2, so v = √62.8 = 7.92 m/s. The shape of the track does not matter, only the drop in height. 9.90 m/s comes from using the full 5 m, and 5.94 m/s from using only 1.8 m. 11.6 m/s comes from adding the heights (6.8 m).

mech-w6-q5.question: A 5 kg block starts sliding on a horizontal floor at 6 m/s, with μk = 0.3. How far does it travel before stopping? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w6-q5.explanation: Work–energy: ½mv² = μk·mg·d, so d = v²/(2μk·g) = 36/(2 × 0.3 × 9.81) = 6.12 m. The mass cancels. 12.2 m comes from forgetting the ½, and 60.0 m from forgetting g (36/0.6).

mech-w6-q6.question: A 4 kg block is released from rest 0.2 m above a vertical spring (k = 4000 N/m, at its natural length). What is the maximum compression of the spring? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w6-q6.explanation: Total drop = 0.2 + x. Energy: ½·4000·x² = 4·9.81·(0.2 + x), i.e. 2000x² − 39.24x − 7.848 = 0. The positive root is x = (39.24 + √(39.24² + 4·2000·7.848))/4000 = 0.0732 m = 73.2 mm. 62.6 mm comes from ignoring the extra drop x during compression and using only mg·0.2 = ½kx². 9.8 mm is just the static deflection mg/k.

mech-w6-q7.question: A trolley is pulled by a 50 N force that makes 60° with its displacement. The trolley moves 4 m. How much work does this force do?
mech-w6-q7.explanation: U = F·d·cosθ = 50 × 4 × cos60° = 100 J. 200 J comes from forgetting the angle. 173.2 J comes from using sin instead of cos — the sin component is perpendicular to the displacement and does no work. 12.5 J divides the force by the distance.

mech-w6-q8.question: A motor pulls a cart with a constant 200 N force at a constant 3 m/s (force and velocity in the same direction). What is the motor's power output?
mech-w6-q8.explanation: P = F·v = 200 × 3 = 600 W. 66.7 W comes from dividing F by v. 1800 W comes from squaring v (200 × 9). 200 W takes the force as the power.

mech-w6-q9.question: A block slides 5 m along a horizontal floor. How much work does the floor's normal reaction N do during this?
mech-w6-q9.explanation: The normal reaction is vertical and the displacement horizontal — they are perpendicular, so U = N·d·cos90° = 0. "N × 5" just multiplies force by displacement without looking at directions, and adding a minus does not fix the angle issue. μk·N × 5 is the (magnitude of the) work of friction, which is a different force.

mech-w6-q10.question: A 2 kg pendulum bob hangs on a 1.5 m string. With the string held horizontal, the bob is released from rest. What is its speed at the lowest point? (g = 9.81 m/s², neglect air resistance)
mech-w6-q10.explanation: The tension is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work; only gravity does: ½v² = g × 1.5, v = √(2 × 9.81 × 1.5) = 5.42 m/s. 3.84 m/s comes from forgetting the 2 (√(gL)). 29.4 comes from not taking the square root (2gL = 29.4 m²/s²). 7.67 m/s comes from taking the drop as 2L = 3 m.

mech-w6-q11.question: A spring with k = 800 N/m is compressed 0.1 m with a 0.2 kg ball in front of it (frictionless horizontal surface). At what speed does the ball leave when the spring is released?
mech-w6-q11.explanation: ½kx² = ½mv², so the spring energy is 4 J and v = x√(k/m) = 0.1 × √4000 = 6.32 m/s. 4.47 m/s comes from putting ½ on one side only (½kx² = mv²). 40.0 comes from forgetting the square root (v² = 40). 8.94 m/s comes from dropping the ½ in the spring energy (kx² = ½mv²).

mech-w6-q12.question: A 4 kg block is released from rest at the top of a 30° incline and slides 5 m along it to the bottom. μk = 0.2. What is its speed at the bottom? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w6-q12.explanation: Height drop = 5 sin30° = 2.5 m, so gravity does 39.24 × 2.5 = 98.1 J. Friction = μk·mg cos30° = 0.2 × 39.24 × 0.866 = 6.80 N, doing −6.80 × 5 = −34.0 J. ½ × 4 × v² = 98.1 − 34.0 = 64.1 J, so v = 5.66 m/s. 7.00 m/s comes from forgetting friction. 5.42 m/s comes from dropping cos30° in the friction (N = mg). 9.01 m/s comes from taking the 5 m incline length as the height.

mech-w6-q13.question: A 2 kg block is released from rest on a frictionless 30° incline. After sliding 1 m it hits a spring lying along the incline (k = 1000 N/m, at natural length). What is the maximum compression of the spring? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w6-q13.explanation: The total travel along the incline is 1 + x, so the height drop is (1 + x) sin30°. Energy: mg(1 + x) sin30° = ½kx² ⇒ 9.81(1 + x) = 500x², i.e. 500x² − 9.81x − 9.81 = 0. Positive root: x = (9.81 + √(9.81² + 4 × 500 × 9.81))/1000 = 0.150 m = 150 mm. 140 mm comes from forgetting the extra drop during compression (x). 219 mm comes from using the full mg without sin30°, and 9.8 mm is only the static compression (mg sin30°/k).

mech-w6-q14.question: A 0.5 kg block on a rough horizontal floor (μk = 0.3) is attached to a spring (k = 300 N/m). The spring is compressed 0.1 m and the block released from rest. What is the block's speed when the spring reaches its natural length? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w6-q14.explanation: Spring energy = ½ × 300 × 0.1² = 1.5 J. Work of friction = −μk·mg·d = −0.3 × 0.5 × 9.81 × 0.1 = −0.147 J. ½ × 0.5 × v² = 1.5 − 0.147 = 1.353 J, so v = 2.33 m/s. 2.45 m/s comes from forgetting friction. 2.57 m/s comes from taking friction's work as positive (adding it). 1.64 m/s comes from dropping the ½ in the KE (mv² = 1.353).

mech-w6-q15.question: A 1000 kg car climbs a 5° slope at a constant 20 m/s. Rolling resistance plus air drag total 300 N (opposing motion). What power must the engine deliver at the wheels? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w6-q15.explanation: The speed is constant, so the driving force = mg sin5° + 300 = 9810 × 0.0872 + 300 = 855 + 300 = 1155 N. P = F·v = 1155 × 20 = 23.1 kW. 6.0 kW is the resistance alone (300 × 20), forgetting the slope. 17.1 kW is the gravity part alone. 202 kW comes from using the whole weight (9810 N) instead of mg sin5°.

mech-w7-q1.question: When applying the principle of virtual work to an ideal mechanism (smooth pins, rollers, rigid inextensible links), which forces automatically do zero virtual work?
options: The reactions at smooth pins and rollers
mech-w7-q1.explanation: A smooth pin's reaction acts at a point that does not move, and a roller's reaction is perpendicular to the motion — both do zero virtual work. That is why the method skips them without solving for them. Friction is non-ideal: it does work during sliding, so it has to be included separately.

mech-w7-q2.question: A lever is pivoted at fulcrum O. Effort P acts 1.2 m from O and an 800 N load acts 0.3 m from O on the other side (both forces perpendicular to the lever). Using a virtual rotation δθ, find P for equilibrium.
mech-w7-q2.explanation: For a virtual rotation δθ, the effort point moves 1.2·δθ and the load point 0.3·δθ. δU = P·1.2·δθ − 800·0.3·δθ = 0, so P = 240/1.2 = 200 N. 3200 N comes from swapping the arms (800 × 1.2/0.3). A longer effort arm reduces the force, not increases it.

mech-w7-q3.question: Scissor linkage: bars AB = BC = L, hinged at B, A pinned to the floor, C on a roller on the floor, both bars at θ = 45° to the floor. A 200 N vertical load acts down at B. What horizontal force Q at C (towards A) keeps equilibrium?
mech-w7-q3.explanation: y_B = L sinθ, x_C = 2L cosθ. δU = −200·L cosθ·δθ + Q·2L sinθ·δθ = 0, so Q = 200/(2 tanθ) = 200/2 = 100 N. 200 N comes from dropping the 2 in x_C = 2L cosθ and using x_C = L cosθ. 141.4 N = 200/√2, just a component of the load.

mech-w7-q4.question: In a linkage the slider position is x = 2L cosθ, with L = 0.5 m. At θ = 30°, for a virtual rotation δθ = 0.01 rad, what is the slider's virtual displacement δx?
mech-w7-q4.explanation: δx = (dx/dθ)·δθ = −2L sinθ·δθ = −2 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.01 = −0.005 m. The minus sign means the slider moves towards the origin as θ increases. −0.00866 m comes from taking d(cosθ)/dθ as −cosθ instead of −sinθ, and +0.005 m from dropping the minus sign.

mech-w7-q5.question: The potential energy of a conservative system is V(x) = 2x³ − 6x joules (x in metres). What is true about its equilibrium positions and their stability?
mech-w7-q5.explanation: dV/dx = 6x² − 6 = 0 ⇒ x = ±1. d²V/dx² = 12x: at x = 1 it is +12 > 0 (V minimum, stable), at x = −1 it is −12 < 0 (V maximum, unstable). The reversed answer comes from remembering 'negative V'' = stable' — in fact a minimum (positive curvature) is stable, like a ball at the bottom of a bowl. At x = 0, dV/dx = −6 ≠ 0, so it is not an equilibrium.

mech-w7-q6.question: Scissor linkage: AB = BC = 0.5 m, A pinned to the floor, C on a roller on the floor, a 100 N vertical load down at B. Instead of a force Q, a horizontal spring connects A and C; its natural length is 0.5 m (which is AC at θ = 60°). What spring constant k gives equilibrium at θ = 30°? (bars weightless)
mech-w7-q6.explanation: By virtual work the spring must pull C with Q = P/(2 tanθ) = 100/(2 tan30°) = 86.6 N. At θ = 30°, AC = 2 × 0.5 × cos30° = 0.866 m, so the stretch = 0.866 − 0.5 = 0.366 m. k = 86.6/0.366 = 237 N/m. 473 N/m comes from dropping the 2 in x_C and using Q = P/tanθ. 100 N/m comes from dividing by the full length 0.866 m instead of the stretch.

mech-w7-q7.question: In the principle of virtual work, what is a "virtual displacement"?
options: The actual displacement the body undergoes over some time under the loads
Only a virtual rotation; translation is not allowed in this method
A large, finite displacement in the direction of the load
An imaginary, very small, constraint-compatible displacement
mech-w7-q7.explanation: A virtual displacement δq is a thinking tool: imaginary, infinitesimal, and it respects the constraints (rotation about a pin, sliding along a roller). It is not the real motion, so no time passes. Both translation and rotation are allowed. A "large, finite" displacement is wrong, because the geometry itself would change.

mech-w7-q8.question: A couple M = 50 N·m acts on a body, and the body makes a virtual rotation δθ = 0.02 rad in the same sense as the couple. What is the couple's virtual work?
mech-w7-q8.explanation: Virtual work of a couple = M·δθ = 50 × 0.02 = 1.0 J (N·m × rad = J). 2500 J comes from dividing by δθ. 0 J is wrong — a couple has zero net force, but it does work through a rotation. 0.5 J adds a ½ that does not belong, as if it were spring energy.

mech-w7-q9.question: A conservative system has potential energy V(q) = 5q² − 20q joules. What is the equilibrium position and its stability?
mech-w7-q9.explanation: dV/dq = 10q − 20 = 0 ⇒ q = 2. d²V/dq² = 10 > 0, so V is a minimum and the equilibrium is stable. q = 4 comes from setting V = 0 (5q² = 20q) — equilibrium comes from dV/dq = 0, not V = 0. At q = 0, dV/dq = −20 ≠ 0. Positive curvature = stable, so "unstable" is wrong.

mech-w7-q10.question: In a linkage the height of the load point is y = L sinθ, with L = 0.8 m. For a virtual rotation δθ = 0.02 rad at θ = 60°, what is δy?
mech-w7-q10.explanation: δy = (dy/dθ)·δθ = L cosθ·δθ = 0.8 × 0.5 × 0.02 = 0.008 m. 0.0139 m comes from putting sin instead of cos in the derivative. −0.008 m is wrong: the derivative of sin is +cos; the minus belongs to the derivative of cos. 0.016 m comes from forgetting cos60°.

mech-w7-q11.question: Scissor linkage: bars AB = BC = L, hinged at B, A pinned to the floor, C on a roller on the floor. Both bars make θ = 60° with the floor. A 240 N vertical load acts downward at B. What horizontal force Q at C (toward A) keeps it in equilibrium? (bars weightless)
mech-w7-q11.explanation: y_B = L sinθ, x_C = 2L cosθ. δU = −240·L cosθ·δθ + Q·2L sinθ·δθ = 0 ⇒ Q = 240/(2 tan60°) = 240/3.464 = 69.3 N. 207.8 N comes from putting tan in the numerator (P tanθ/2). 138.6 N comes from forgetting the 2 in x_C (P/tanθ). 120 N is just P/2, ignoring the angle.

mech-w7-q12.question: A uniform bar AB, 2 m long and weighing 50 N, has its lower end A pinned to the floor. The bar is at θ = 30° to the floor, and a horizontal force P at the top end B (pointing toward the vertical line through A) stops it falling. Find P by virtual work. (no friction)
mech-w7-q12.explanation: Take the origin at A. The weight acts at G: y_G = 1·sinθ, so δy_G = cosθ·δθ. B: x_B = 2 cosθ, δx_B = −2 sinθ·δθ. P points in −x, so its work = −P·δx_B = 2P sinθ·δθ. δU = −50 cosθ·δθ + 2P sinθ·δθ = 0 ⇒ P = 50/(2 tan30°) = 43.3 N. 86.6 N comes from placing the weight at B (y = 2 sinθ) instead of G. 14.4 N comes from inverting the tan (25 tan30°). 25.0 N is W/2, ignoring the angle.

mech-w7-q13.question: A light rod (length L = 0.5 m) carries a 2 kg mass at its top, and the rod is joined at its lower pin by a torsional spring (stiffness k, N·m/rad). At angle θ from the vertical, V(θ) = ½kθ² + mgL cosθ. How large must k be for the vertical position (θ = 0) to be stable? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w7-q13.explanation: dV/dθ = kθ − mgL sinθ, which is zero at θ = 0, so this is an equilibrium. d²V/dθ² = k − mgL cosθ; at θ = 0 we need k − mgL > 0, i.e. k > 2 × 9.81 × 0.5 = 9.81 N·m/rad. 19.62 comes from forgetting L and using just mg. 4.905 adds a ½ that does not belong. "Any k" is wrong: if k is small, the −mgL term makes V a maximum (unstable).

mech-w7-q14.question: Scissor linkage: bars AB = BC = L, each a uniform bar weighing 80 N, A pinned to the floor, C on a roller on the smooth floor, hinged at B. Both bars are at θ = 45° to the floor, and there is no other load. What horizontal force Q at C (toward A) keeps it in equilibrium?
mech-w7-q14.explanation: Each bar's centre is at height (L/2) sinθ, so each weight does virtual work −80·(L/2) cosθ·δθ. x_C = 2L cosθ. δU = −2 × 80 × (L/2) cosθ·δθ + Q·2L sinθ·δθ = 0 ⇒ Q = 80/(2 tanθ) = 40 N (θ = 45°). 80 N comes from putting both weights at B (height L sinθ). 20 N counts only one bar's weight. 56.6 N just takes the cos45° component of a weight.

mech-w7-q15.question: A uniform crank OA (length 0.6 m, weight 40 N) is pinned at O and sits at θ = 60° above the horizontal. A 200 N vertical force acts downward at end A. What couple M at O (in the direction that increases θ) holds the crank in this position?
mech-w7-q15.explanation: y_A = 0.6 sinθ, y_G = 0.3 sinθ. δU = M·δθ − 200 × 0.6 cosθ·δθ − 40 × 0.3 cosθ·δθ = 0 ⇒ M = (120 + 12) cos60° = 66.0 N·m. 60.0 N·m comes from forgetting the crank's own weight. 114.3 N·m comes from using sin instead of cos (132 × 0.866). 72.0 N·m comes from putting the crank's weight at A instead of G ((200 + 40) × 0.6 × 0.5).

mech-w8-q1.question: A 20 kg crate is pulled across a horizontal floor by a 100 N horizontal force. μk = 0.2. What is the crate's acceleration? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w8-q1.explanation: Friction = μk·mg = 0.2 × 20 × 9.81 = 39.24 N. a = (100 − 39.24)/20 = 3.04 m/s². 5.00 m/s² comes from forgetting friction, and 6.96 m/s² from adding friction to the pull — friction opposes the motion.

mech-w8-q2.question: A car moves at a constant speed of 20 m/s around a curve of radius 80 m. What is its normal (centripetal) acceleration?
mech-w8-q2.explanation: a_n = v²/ρ = 20²/80 = 400/80 = 5 m/s². The speed is constant so a_t = 0, but a_n is not zero. 0.25 m/s² comes from v/ρ (forgetting the square), and 4 m/s² from ρ/v.

mech-w8-q3.question: A car is on a curve of radius 75 m. At this instant its speed is 15 m/s and it is speeding up at 3 m/s². What is the magnitude of its total acceleration?
mech-w8-q3.explanation: a_t = 3 m/s², a_n = 15²/75 = 3 m/s². They are perpendicular, so |a| = √(3² + 3²) = √18 = 4.24 m/s². 6.00 m/s² comes from adding them directly (not as vectors), and 18.0 from forgetting the square root. 3.00 is just one component.

mech-w8-q4.question: A bead slides along a rotating rod. At this instant r = 0.5 m, ṙ = 0.2 m/s, r̈ = 0, θ̇ = 4 rad/s and θ̈ = 0. What is the transverse acceleration a_θ?
mech-w8-q4.explanation: a_θ = r·θ̈ + 2·ṙ·θ̇ = 0.5 × 0 + 2 × 0.2 × 4 = 1.6 m/s². Even with θ̈ = 0 the 2ṙθ̇ term remains — '0' is exactly the trap. 0.8 m/s² comes from forgetting the 2, and 2.0 m/s² is v_θ = rθ̇, a velocity, not an acceleration.

mech-w8-q5.question: At what angle should a road of radius 100 m be banked so that a car at 25 m/s needs no friction at all? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w8-q5.explanation: Without friction: N sinθ = mv²/r and N cosθ = mg, so tanθ = v²/(g·r) = 625/981 = 0.637, θ = 32.5°. 39.6° comes from sin⁻¹(0.637) — the wrong function. 57.5° is the complement, which you get by measuring from the vertical. 14.0° is tan⁻¹(v/r), which drops both the square on v and g.

mech-w8-q6.question: Block A (6 kg) is on a horizontal table (μk = 0.2) and is tied by a light string that passes over a smooth pulley at the table's edge to a hanging block B (4 kg). When the system is released, what is the tension in the string? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w8-q6.explanation: For the whole system: a = (4·9.81 − 0.2·6·9.81)/(6 + 4) = (39.24 − 11.77)/10 = 2.75 m/s². Block B: 4·9.81 − T = 4a, so T = 4(9.81 − 2.75) = 28.3 N (check with A: T = 6a + 11.77 = 28.3 ✓). 39.2 N is B's weight — the block is accelerating, so T is less than its weight. 23.5 N comes from forgetting friction.

mech-w8-q7.question: A net braking force of 6000 N acts on a 1500 kg car. What is its deceleration?
mech-w8-q7.explanation: ΣF = m·a ⇒ a = 6000/1500 = 4.00 m/s². 0.25 m/s² comes from dividing the wrong way (m/F). 40.0 m/s² is a misplaced decimal point. 9.81 m/s² is g, which plays no role in this horizontal motion.

mech-w8-q8.question: A ball is thrown horizontally from the top of a 20 m tall building. How long does it take to reach the ground? (g = 9.81 m/s², neglect air resistance)
mech-w8-q8.explanation: The initial vertical velocity is zero (horizontal throw): 20 = ½ × 9.81 × t², t = √(40/9.81) = 2.02 s. The horizontal speed does not affect this time. 4.08 s comes from forgetting the square root (t² = 4.08). 1.43 s comes from dropping the ½ (h = g·t²), and 1.01 s from inverting the formula to √(h/2g).

mech-w8-q9.question: A bead is held at r = 2 m on a rotating rod (ṙ = 0), and the rod turns at θ̇ = 3 rad/s. What is the bead's transverse velocity v_θ?
mech-w8-q9.explanation: v_θ = r·θ̇ = 2 × 3 = 6 m/s. 0 m/s is wrong: ṙ = 0 only makes the radial velocity zero. 18 m/s = rθ̇², which is the centripetal acceleration (m/s²), not a velocity. 1.5 m/s is r/θ̇.

mech-w8-q10.question: A 70 kg man stands on a weighing scale in a lift that is accelerating upward at 2 m/s². What reading (normal force) does the scale show? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w8-q10.explanation: ΣFy = m·a: N − mg = m·a, so N = 70(9.81 + 2) = 827 N. 687 N is just the weight (as if a = 0). 547 N comes from taking the acceleration as downward (9.81 − 2). 140 N is only m·a, forgetting the weight.

mech-w8-q11.question: A roller-coaster car is at the top of a vertical loop of radius 10 m. What minimum speed keeps it in contact with the track at the top? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w8-q11.explanation: At the top, N and mg both point down (toward the centre): N + mg = mv²/r. At the minimum speed N = 0, so v = √(g·r) = √98.1 = 9.90 m/s. 14.0 m/s = √(2gr), a mix-up with the energy formula. 98.1 comes from forgetting the square root (v² = 98.1). 4.95 m/s halves the answer for no reason.

mech-w8-q12.question: A slider moves along a rotating arm. At this instant r = 0.4 m, ṙ = 0.5 m/s, r̈ = 0.2 m/s², θ̇ = 3 rad/s and θ̈ = 1 rad/s². What is the magnitude of the slider's total acceleration?
mech-w8-q12.explanation: a_r = r̈ − r·θ̇² = 0.2 − 0.4 × 9 = −3.4 m/s². a_θ = r·θ̈ + 2ṙθ̇ = 0.4 + 2 × 0.5 × 3 = 3.4 m/s². |a| = √(3.4² + 3.4²) = 4.81 m/s². 3.89 m/s² comes from dropping the factor 2 in 2ṙθ̇ (a_θ = 1.9). 6.80 m/s² adds the perpendicular components directly. 5.10 m/s² comes from taking −rθ̇² as + (a_r = 3.8).

mech-w8-q13.question: A road of radius 60 m is banked at 20°, with μs = 0.3 between tyres and road. What is the maximum speed at which a car can take the turn without sliding up the slope? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w8-q13.explanation: At maximum speed, friction acts down the slope (toward the centre). Vertical: N cos20° − μN sin20° = mg. Horizontal: N sin20° + μN cos20° = mv²/r. Dividing, v² = g·r(sin20° + μ cos20°)/(cos20° − μ sin20°) = 588.6 × 0.624/0.837 = 438.7, so v = 20.9 m/s. 14.6 m/s is the frictionless (tanθ) speed. 13.3 m/s is the flat-road √(μgr), forgetting the banking. 19.8 m/s comes from simply adding tanθ and μ (√(gr(tanθ + μ))).

mech-w8-q14.question: Block A (5 kg) is on a frictionless 30° incline, tied to a light string that runs over a smooth pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block B (4 kg). When released, what is the system's acceleration? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w8-q14.explanation: Driving force = weight of B − component of A's weight along the slope = 4 × 9.81 − 5 × 9.81 × sin30° = 39.24 − 24.53 = 14.72 N. a = 14.72/(5 + 4) = 1.64 m/s² (B down, A up). 4.36 m/s² comes from forgetting A's slope component (39.24/9). 2.94 m/s² divides by A's mass alone. 1.09 m/s² comes from using A's full weight without sin30° (and then the direction comes out reversed too).

mech-w8-q15.question: A ball is thrown from the ground at 20 m/s at 45° above the horizontal. A wall stands 30 m from the launch point. What is the ball's height when it reaches the wall? (g = 9.81 m/s², neglect air resistance)
mech-w8-q15.explanation: v_x = v_y0 = 20 cos45° = 14.14 m/s. Time to the wall t = 30/14.14 = 2.12 s. y = 14.14 × 2.12 − ½ × 9.81 × 2.12² = 30.0 − 22.1 = 7.93 m. 30.0 m comes from forgetting gravity. 22.1 m is only the drop due to gravity. 10.2 m comes from dropping cos45° in the horizontal speed (v_x = 20, t = 1.5 s).

mech-w9-q1.question: A satellite is in an elliptical orbit. At perigee its distance (from Earth's centre) is 7000 km and its speed is 8 km/s. Apogee is at 14000 km. What is the speed at apogee?
mech-w9-q1.explanation: At perigee and apogee the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so angular momentum gives r_p·v_p = r_a·v_a: v_a = 7000 × 8/14000 = 4 km/s. 16 km/s comes from inverting the ratio — the speed is lower at the far point. 5.66 km/s (= 8/√2) comes from applying the circular-orbit √(1/r) scaling.

mech-w9-q2.question: A particle is acted on only by a central force that always points towards a fixed point O. Which quantity is necessarily conserved about O?
mech-w9-q2.explanation: A central force has zero moment about O (it passes through O), so the angular momentum H_O = m·r²θ̇ stays constant. Linear momentum is not conserved because the net force is not zero. Speed also changes in an elliptical orbit — it is constant only in a circular orbit.

mech-w9-q3.question: What is the speed of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius 8000 km measured from Earth's centre? (GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²)
mech-w9-q3.explanation: v = √(GM/r) = √(3.986 × 10¹⁴ / 8 × 10⁶) = √(4.98 × 10⁷) = 7059 m/s ≈ 7.06 km/s. 9.98 km/s is the escape speed √(2GM/r) at this radius. 49.8 comes from forgetting the square root (GM/r = 49.8 km²/s²).

mech-w9-q4.question: A satellite's circular orbit radius is made 4 times larger (same planet). By what factor does its orbital period change?
mech-w9-q4.explanation: T = 2π√(r³/GM), so T ∝ r^(3/2). r × 4 ⇒ T × 4^(3/2) = 8 times. 4 times assumes T ∝ r, 16 times assumes T ∝ r², and 2 times assumes T ∝ √r. Remember Kepler's third law T² ∝ r³.

mech-w9-q5.question: The circular orbit speed at radius r is 7.5 km/s. What is the escape speed from that same radius?
mech-w9-q5.explanation: v_circ = √(GM/r) and v_esc = √(2GM/r), so v_esc = √2 × 7.5 = 10.6 km/s. 15.0 km/s comes from multiplying by 2 instead of √2. 11.2 km/s is the memorised escape speed at Earth's surface — it does not apply at this radius.

mech-w9-q6.question: A satellite's elliptical orbit has perigee 6800 km and apogee 12000 km (both from Earth's centre). What is its speed at perigee? (GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²)
mech-w9-q6.explanation: a = (6800 + 12000)/2 = 9400 km. Vis-viva: v_p² = GM(2/r_p − 1/a) = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ × (2/6.8 × 10⁶ − 1/9.4 × 10⁶) = 7.483 × 10⁷, so v_p = 8650 m/s ≈ 8.65 km/s. 7.66 km/s is the circular speed at 6800 km — the perigee speed of an ellipse is higher than that. 9.17 km/s comes from putting r_a in place of a in the formula, and 10.8 km/s is the escape speed.

mech-w9-q7.question: At which point of an elliptical orbit is a satellite's speed the greatest?
options: Between the two, at the semi-minor axis
mech-w9-q7.explanation: h = r·v⊥ is constant, so the speed is greatest where r is smallest (perigee). Kepler's second law says the same: near the planet it must move faster to sweep equal areas in equal times. Equal speed holds only in a circular orbit, and at apogee the speed is the lowest.

mech-w9-q8.question: A satellite's orbit has perigee radius 7000 km and apogee radius 15000 km (both from Earth's centre). What is the semi-major axis a?
mech-w9-q8.explanation: a = (r_p + r_a)/2 = (7000 + 15000)/2 = 11000 km. 4000 km is half the difference. 22000 km is the sum, without halving. 10247 km is the geometric mean √(r_p·r_a), which gives the semi-minor axis b, not a.

mech-w9-q9.question: A satellite is in a circular orbit 600 km above Earth's surface (Earth radius 6371 km). What value of r goes into the orbit equations?
mech-w9-q9.explanation: r is always measured from Earth's centre: r = R + h = 6371 + 600 = 6971 km. 600 km is only the altitude — the most common trap. 5771 km is R − h, and 12742 km is Earth's diameter.

mech-w9-q10.question: What is the period of a circular orbit of radius 7000 km (from Earth's centre)? (GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²)
mech-w9-q10.explanation: T = 2π√(r³/GM) = 2π√((7 × 10⁶)³/3.986 × 10¹⁴) = 2π × 927.6 = 5828 s = 97.1 min. 15.5 min comes from forgetting the 2π (927.6 s). 48.6 min comes from using π instead of 2π, and 194 min from using 4π.

mech-w9-q11.question: A 500 kg satellite is in a circular orbit of radius 7000 km (from Earth's centre). What is its total mechanical energy? (GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²)
mech-w9-q11.explanation: E = −GMm/(2a), and in a circular orbit a = r: E = −3.986 × 10¹⁴ × 500/(2 × 7 × 10⁶) = −1.42 × 10¹⁰ J. −2.85 × 10¹⁰ J is only the potential energy (−GMm/r), missing the 2. The positive value is the kinetic energy — the total energy of a bound orbit is always negative. −7.12 × 10⁹ J applies the 2 twice.

mech-w9-q12.question: A satellite has perigee radius 6800 km and apogee radius 12000 km (from Earth's centre). What is its speed at apogee? (GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²)
mech-w9-q12.explanation: a = (6800 + 12000)/2 = 9400 km. Vis-viva: v_a² = GM(2/r_a − 1/a) = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ × (2/1.2 × 10⁷ − 1/9.4 × 10⁶) = 2.40 × 10⁷, so v_a = 4.90 km/s. (Check: v_p = 8.65 km/s, and 6800 × 8.65 ≈ 12000 × 4.90 ✓.) 5.76 km/s is the circular speed at 12000 km — the ellipse is slower than that at apogee. 15.3 km/s comes from inverting the angular-momentum ratio, and 6.51 km/s is the circular speed at r = a.

mech-w9-q13.question: A geostationary satellite has a period of 1 sidereal day = 86164 s. Roughly what is its altitude (above Earth's surface)? (GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², Earth radius 6371 km)
mech-w9-q13.explanation: T = 2π√(r³/GM) ⇒ r = (GM·T²/4π²)^(1/3) = (3.986 × 10¹⁴ × 86164²/39.48)^(1/3) = 4.216 × 10⁷ m ≈ 42,200 km. Altitude = r − R = 42,164 − 6371 ≈ 35,800 km. 42,200 km is the orbit radius, not the altitude (forgetting to subtract R). 26,600 km is the radius of a 12-hour orbit (halving T). 6,400 km is just Earth's radius.

mech-w9-q14.question: A satellite wants to move by a Hohmann transfer from a circular LEO of radius 6771 km to a geostationary orbit of radius 42164 km. What is the first burn (Δv₁) at LEO? (GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²)
mech-w9-q14.explanation: Transfer ellipse: r_p = 6771 km, r_a = 42164 km, so a = 24467.5 km. LEO speed v₁ = √(GM/r₁) = 7.67 km/s. Perigee speed on the ellipse (vis-viva) = √(GM(2/r₁ − 1/a)) = 10.07 km/s. Δv₁ = 10.07 − 7.67 = 2.40 km/s. 10.07 km/s is the whole perigee speed, not the change. 4.60 km/s is the difference of the two circular speeds — a Hohmann transfer has no such single burn. 3.07 km/s is the circular speed at GEO.

mech-w9-q15.question: A satellite is in a circular orbit of radius 7000 km (from Earth's centre). From that point, what extra (tangential) increase in speed is needed to escape Earth's gravity? (GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²)
mech-w9-q15.explanation: v_c = √(GM/r) = √(3.986 × 10¹⁴/7 × 10⁶) = 7.55 km/s. v_esc = √2 × v_c = 10.67 km/s. Extra Δv = 10.67 − 7.55 = 3.13 km/s (= (√2 − 1)v_c). 10.7 km/s is the full escape speed, not the increase. 11.2 km/s is the memorised surface value, not for this r. 7.55 km/s is just the circular speed.

mech-w10-q1.question: A wheel of radius 0.3 m rolls without slipping with its centre moving at 6 m/s. What is the speed of the topmost point of the wheel?
mech-w10-q1.explanation: The IC is the contact point. ω = v/R = 6/0.3 = 20 rad/s. The top point is 2R = 0.6 m from the IC, so v = 20 × 0.6 = 12 m/s (= 2 × centre speed). 6 m/s is the centre's speed. 0 is the contact point's. 8.49 m/s (= 6√2) is the speed of a side point level with the centre.

mech-w10-q2.question: A disc starts from rest and spins with a constant angular acceleration of 4 rad/s². After 3 s, what is the speed of a point 0.5 m from the axis?
mech-w10-q2.explanation: ω = ω₀ + αt = 0 + 4 × 3 = 12 rad/s. v = ω·r = 12 × 0.5 = 6 m/s. 12 is ω (rad/s), not a speed. 9 m/s comes from multiplying the angle θ = ½·4·3² = 18 rad by r — that is an arc length (m). 2 m/s is α·r, which is the tangential acceleration (m/s²).

mech-w10-q3.question: A 5 m ladder has its top A sliding on a vertical wall and its bottom B on the floor. When A is 4 m above the floor and B is 3 m from the wall, B moves away from the wall at 2 m/s. What is the speed of A?
mech-w10-q3.explanation: The IC is at (3, 4). Its distance to B is 4 m, so ω = 2/4 = 0.5 rad/s. Its distance to A is 3 m, so v_A = 0.5 × 3 = 1.5 m/s (downward). From the constraint as well: x·ẋ + y·ẏ = 0 ⇒ ẏ = −3 × 2/4 = −1.5 ✓. 2.67 m/s comes from inverting the ratio (2 × 4/3). 0.5 is ω.

mech-w10-q4.question: A 1 m bar AB is horizontal at this instant, with B to the right of A. A's velocity is 3 m/s to the right and the bar rotates counter-clockwise at 2 rad/s. What is the speed of B?
mech-w10-q4.explanation: v_B = v_A + ω × r_B/A. r_B/A = 1 m to the right, and CCW rotation gives ω × r = 2 × 1 = 2 m/s upward. So v_B = (3 right, 2 up), |v_B| = √(3² + 2²) = 3.61 m/s. 5.00 m/s comes from adding perpendicular vectors as scalars, and 1.00 m/s from subtracting them.

mech-w10-q5.question: A disc rotates about a fixed axis. At this instant ω = 5 rad/s and α = 10 rad/s². What is the magnitude of the total acceleration of a point 0.2 m from the axis?
mech-w10-q5.explanation: a_n = ω²r = 25 × 0.2 = 5 m/s² (towards the axis), a_t = αr = 10 × 0.2 = 2 m/s². They are perpendicular: |a| = √(5² + 2²) = 5.39 m/s². 7.00 m/s² comes from adding them directly. 5.00 and 2.00 are just the individual components.

mech-w10-q6.question: A horizontal disc rotates at a constant Ω = 2 rad/s. A slider moves outward in a radial slot of the disc at a constant relative speed of 1 m/s. When the slider is 0.5 m from the centre, what is the magnitude of its absolute acceleration?
mech-w10-q6.explanation: Ω̇ = 0, a_rel = 0. Centripetal Ω²r = 4 × 0.5 = 2 m/s² (towards the centre). Coriolis 2Ω·v_rel = 2 × 2 × 1 = 4 m/s² (perpendicular to the radius). |a| = √(2² + 4²) = 4.47 m/s². 2.00 m/s² comes from forgetting Coriolis, 2.83 m/s² from dropping its factor 2 (√(2² + 2²)), and 6.00 m/s² from adding perpendicular components.

mech-w10-q7.question: A pulley turns at 120 rpm. What is the speed of a point on its rim 0.25 m from the axis?
mech-w10-q7.explanation: ω = 120 × 2π/60 = 12.57 rad/s, v = ω·r = 12.57 × 0.25 = 3.14 m/s. 30.0 m/s comes from multiplying rpm directly by r — convert to rad/s first. 12.6 is ω (rad/s), not a speed. 0.50 m/s takes rev/s (2) × r, forgetting the 2π.

mech-w10-q8.question: A body is in curvilinear translation (like a Ferris wheel seat). Which is true?
options: Every point moves on a circle, so ω ≠ 0
Only the centre of mass has a defined velocity
The speed of points grows with distance from the centre
Every point has the same velocity, ω = 0
mech-w10-q8.explanation: In translation the body does not rotate (ω = 0), so every point has the same velocity and acceleration — even on a curved path. Each point of the seat moves on a circle, but all those circles are the same size and the seat's lines stay parallel to themselves. Speed growing with distance is a feature of rotation, not translation.

mech-w10-q9.question: A wheel of radius 0.4 m rolls without slipping, with its centre moving at 2 m/s. What is the wheel's angular velocity?
mech-w10-q9.explanation: Rolling without slipping: v = ω·R, so ω = 2/0.4 = 5 rad/s. 0.8 rad/s comes from v × R. 2.5 rad/s is just 1/R, forgetting the speed. 10 rad/s divides the top point's speed (2v = 4 m/s) by R.

mech-w10-q10.question: A flywheel running at 300 rpm comes to rest in 10 s with constant deceleration. How many revolutions does it make before stopping?
mech-w10-q10.explanation: ω₀ = 300 × 2π/60 = 31.4 rad/s. With constant α, θ = ½(ω₀ + 0)·t = ½ × 31.4 × 10 = 157 rad = 157/(2π) = 25 revolutions. 50 comes from using the initial speed (5 rev/s) for the whole 10 s instead of the average. 157 is in radians, not revolutions. 1500 mixes rpm with seconds (300 × 10/2).

mech-w10-q11.question: A 2 m bar AB is vertical at this instant (B above A). A moves right at 4 m/s and the bar rotates clockwise at 1.5 rad/s. What is the velocity of B?
mech-w10-q11.explanation: v_B = v_A + ω × r_B/A. r_B/A = 2 m up. In a clockwise rotation, a point above A moves to the right: ω·r = 1.5 × 2 = 3 m/s right. v_B = 4 + 3 = 7 m/s right. 1 m/s comes from taking the rotation as CCW (4 − 3). 5 m/s treats them as perpendicular, √(4² + 3²) — here both lie along the same (horizontal) line. 3 m/s is only the relative part, and in the wrong direction too.

mech-w10-q12.question: A 4 m ladder slides with its top A on a smooth vertical wall and its bottom B on a smooth floor. When the ladder is at 30° to the floor, B moves away from the wall at 1.5 m/s. What is the speed of A?
mech-w10-q12.explanation: A = (0, 4 sin30°) = (0, 2), B = (4 cos30°, 0) = (3.46, 0). The IC is at (3.46, 2). IC to B is 2 m, so ω = 1.5/2 = 0.75 rad/s. IC to A is 3.46 m, so v_A = 0.75 × 3.46 = 2.60 m/s downward. Constraint check: ẏ = −x·ẋ/y = −3.46 × 1.5/2 = −2.60 ✓. 0.87 m/s inverts the distance ratio. 1.50 m/s assumes both ends move equally fast, and 3.00 m/s multiplies instead of dividing when finding ω (1.5 × 2).

mech-w10-q13.question: A wheel of radius 0.5 m rolls without slipping at a constant 3 m/s. What is the acceleration of the contact point on the ground?
mech-w10-q13.explanation: ω = v/R = 3/0.5 = 6 rad/s; the speed is constant, so α = 0 and a_centre = 0. Contact-point acceleration = a_centre + ω²R (toward the centre) = 6² × 0.5 = 18 m/s² upward. "0" is the big IC mistake — at the IC only the velocity is zero, not the acceleration. 6 m/s² writes ω as the acceleration, and 36 m/s² forgets to multiply ω² by R.

mech-w10-q14.question: A wheel of radius 0.3 m rolls without slipping. At this instant its centre moves at 3 m/s and accelerates at 2 m/s² (forward). What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the topmost point of the wheel?
mech-w10-q14.explanation: ω = 3/0.3 = 10 rad/s, α = 2/0.3 = 6.67 rad/s². Top point (R above the centre): a = a_G (2 forward) + α·R (2 forward) + ω²R (30 down, toward the centre). 4 forward, 30 down: |a| = √(4² + 30²) = 30.3 m/s². 34.0 m/s² adds the perpendicular components directly. 4.0 m/s² forgets the normal term ω²R. 60.0 m/s² uses 2R instead of R in ω²R.

mech-w10-q15.question: A horizontal disc rotates at a constant Ω = 3 rad/s. A slider in its radial slot is 0.4 m from the centre, moving outward at a relative speed of 0.8 m/s with a relative acceleration of 0.5 m/s² (outward). What is the magnitude of the slider's absolute acceleration?
mech-w10-q15.explanation: Radial: a_rel − Ω²r = 0.5 − 9 × 0.4 = −3.1 m/s² (toward the centre). Transverse: Coriolis 2Ω·v_rel = 2 × 3 × 0.8 = 4.8 m/s². |a| = √(3.1² + 4.8²) = 5.71 m/s². 3.92 m/s² comes from dropping the factor 2 in Coriolis (2.4). 6.00 m/s² comes from ignoring a_rel (√(3.6² + 4.8²)). 6.31 m/s² comes from taking a_rel toward the centre (−0.5).

mech-w11-q1.question: A 4 kg solid disc has radius 0.5 m. What is its mass moment of inertia about its central axis (perpendicular to the disc's plane)?
mech-w11-q1.explanation: I = mR²/2 = 4 × 0.25/2 = 0.5 kg·m². 1.0 kg·m² comes from the ring formula mR² — a disc also has mass near the centre, so its I is smaller. 0.25 kg·m² is for a diameter axis (mR²/4).

mech-w11-q2.question: A 2 kg slender rod is 1.5 m long. Using the parallel axis theorem, find I about an axis through one end (perpendicular to the rod).
mech-w11-q2.explanation: I_G = mL²/12 = 2 × 2.25/12 = 0.375. d = L/2 = 0.75 m, so md² = 2 × 0.5625 = 1.125. I_end = 0.375 + 1.125 = 1.5 kg·m² (= mL²/3 ✓). 0.375 is only I_G and 1.125 is only md² — the two must be added.

mech-w11-q3.question: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping down a 30° incline. What is the acceleration of its centre? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w11-q3.explanation: Rolling body: a = g sinθ/(1 + I_G/(mR²)). For a cylinder I_G/(mR²) = 1/2, so a = (2/3) × 9.81 × 0.5 = 3.27 m/s². 4.91 m/s² is frictionless sliding (g sinθ) — ignoring the rotational energy. 2.45 m/s² is the answer for a ring (I/mR² = 1) and 3.50 m/s² for a solid sphere (2/5).

mech-w11-q4.question: A uniform rod 1.5 m long is pinned at one end by a smooth pin and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration at the instant of release? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w11-q4.explanation: ΣM_O = I_O·α: mg(L/2) = (mL²/3)·α, so α = 3g/(2L) = 3 × 9.81/3 = 9.81 rad/s². 39.2 rad/s² comes from using I_G = mL²/12 with moments about the pin. 13.1 rad/s² comes from treating all the mass as a point at the centre (I = m(L/2)²).

mech-w11-q5.question: A 2 kg thin ring (hoop) rolls without slipping at 3 m/s. What is its total kinetic energy?
