mech-w11-q5.explanation: Translational ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J. Rotational ½I_Gω² = ½(mR²)(v/R)² = ½mv² = 9 J. Total = 18 J. 9 J is translation alone. 13.5 J is the answer for a disc (¾mv²) — a ring has all its mass at the rim, so its rotational KE equals its translational KE.

mech-w11-q6.question: A uniform rod 1.2 m long is pinned at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. As the rod swings through the vertical (hanging down) position, what is the speed of its free end? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w11-q6.explanation: G drops by L/2 = 0.6 m. Energy: mg(L/2) = ½(mL²/3)ω², so ω = √(3g/L) = √24.5 = 4.95 rad/s. The free end's speed = ωL = 4.95 × 1.2 = 5.94 m/s. 4.85 m/s (= √(2gL)) comes from treating the end as a freely falling point, and 2.97 m/s is the speed of the centre G (ωL/2).

mech-w11-q7.question: A 3 kg thin ring has radius 0.4 m. What is its mass moment of inertia about its central axis (perpendicular to the plane of the ring)?
mech-w11-q7.explanation: All the ring's mass is on the rim, at distance R: I = mR² = 3 × 0.16 = 0.48 kg·m². 0.24 kg·m² is the disc formula (mR²/2). 0.192 kg·m² is the solid-sphere 2mR²/5. 1.2 kg·m² comes from forgetting to square R (3 × 0.4).

mech-w11-q8.question: A 10 kg body has I = 2.5 kg·m² about some axis. What is its radius of gyration k about that axis?
mech-w11-q8.explanation: I = m·k² ⇒ k = √(I/m) = √0.25 = 0.5 m. 0.25 m comes from forgetting the square root. 4 m comes from dividing the wrong way (m/I). 0.158 m divides by the mass twice (√(2.5/100)).

mech-w11-q9.question: A flywheel has I = 2 kg·m² and a net torque of 10 N·m acts on it. What is its angular acceleration?
mech-w11-q9.explanation: ΣM = I·α ⇒ α = 10/2 = 5 rad/s². 20 rad/s² comes from multiplying the torque by I. 0.2 rad/s² divides the wrong way (I/M). 10 rad/s² ignores I.

mech-w11-q10.question: A 5 kg solid sphere has radius 0.2 m. What is its I about a tangent axis touching the sphere's surface?
mech-w11-q10.explanation: I_G = 2mR²/5 = 2 × 5 × 0.04/5 = 0.08 kg·m². Parallel axis, d = R: I = 0.08 + 5 × 0.04 = 0.28 kg·m². 0.08 is only I_G and 0.20 only md² — they must be added. 0.30 comes from using the disc result mR²/2 for a sphere (0.10 + 0.20).

mech-w11-q11.question: A 10 kg solid disc of radius 0.3 m spins about its central axis at 300 rpm. What is its kinetic energy?
mech-w11-q11.explanation: I = mR²/2 = 10 × 0.09/2 = 0.45 kg·m². ω = 300 × 2π/60 = 31.4 rad/s. T = ½Iω² = ½ × 0.45 × 31.4² = 222 J. 444 J comes from using the ring formula (mR²). 20250 J takes rpm directly as ω (½ × 0.45 × 300²). 111 J uses the diameter-axis I (mR²/4).

mech-w11-q12.question: A pulley is a solid disc (M = 4 kg, R = 0.2 m) turning on a smooth axle. A 2 kg block hangs from a rope wrapped round its rim. When released, what is the block's acceleration? (g = 9.81 m/s², the rope does not slip)
mech-w11-q12.explanation: Block: mg − T = m·a. Pulley: T·R = (MR²/2)·α and a = αR, so T = (M/2)·a = 2a. Adding, 2 × 9.81 = (2 + 2)a, a = 4.91 m/s². 9.81 m/s² forgets the pulley's inertia (free fall). 3.27 m/s² treats the pulley as a ring (I = MR²) (19.62/6). 6.54 m/s² uses I = MR²/4 (19.62/3).

mech-w11-q13.question: Disc A (I = 0.5 kg·m²) spins at 10 rad/s. Disc B (I = 0.3 kg·m²), at rest on the same axis, is dropped onto it and the two then spin together. How much kinetic energy is lost in this process?
mech-w11-q13.explanation: There is no external moment about the axis, so angular momentum is conserved: 0.5 × 10 = 0.8·ω, ω = 6.25 rad/s. KE before = ½ × 0.5 × 100 = 25 J, after = ½ × 0.8 × 6.25² = 15.6 J. Loss = 9.38 J (heat from friction between the discs). 0 J wrongly assumes energy is conserved — here angular momentum is conserved, not KE. 15.6 J is the final KE, not the loss. 19.4 J comes from inverting the ratio (ω = 3.75 rad/s).

mech-w11-q14.question: A solid sphere rolls without slipping from rest down an incline of vertical height 2 m. What is the speed of its centre at the bottom? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w11-q14.explanation: mgh = ½mv² + ½(2mR²/5)(v/R)² = (7/10)mv², so v = √(10gh/7) = √28.0 = 5.29 m/s. 6.26 m/s = √(2gh), forgetting the rotational KE (as in frictionless sliding). 5.11 m/s is the disc/cylinder answer √(4gh/3). 4.43 m/s is the ring's √(gh).

mech-w11-q15.question: A rectangular beam section has width b = 100 mm and depth h = 200 mm. What is its area moment of inertia about the horizontal axis through its base (bottom edge)?
mech-w11-q15.explanation: Centroidal I = bh³/12 = 100 × 200³/12 = 6.67 × 10⁷ mm⁴. The parallel-axis rule works the same for areas: d = h/2 = 100 mm, A = 2 × 10⁴ mm², so I = 6.67 × 10⁷ + 2 × 10⁴ × 100² = 2.67 × 10⁸ mm⁴ (= bh³/3). 6.67 × 10⁷ is just the centroidal I. 1.67 × 10⁷ comes from swapping b and h (hb³/12). 8.67 × 10⁸ comes from taking d = h (200 mm).

mech-w12-q1.question: A 2 kg mass is attached to an 800 N/m spring (no damping). What is the natural frequency fn (in Hz)?
mech-w12-q1.explanation: ωn = √(k/m) = √(800/2) = √400 = 20 rad/s. fn = ωn/(2π) = 20/6.283 = 3.18 Hz. 20.0 Hz comes from writing rad/s directly as Hz — the most common trap. 125.7 Hz comes from multiplying by 2π instead of dividing.

mech-w12-q2.question: Two springs, k₁ = 300 N/m and k₂ = 600 N/m, are connected in series (one below the other) with a mass hanging below them. What is the equivalent stiffness?
mech-w12-q2.explanation: Series: 1/k_eq = 1/300 + 1/600 = 3/600, so k_eq = 200 N/m (= k₁k₂/(k₁ + k₂) = 180000/900). 900 N/m is the parallel formula. In series k_eq is always less than even the softer spring (300), so 300 and 450 are also wrong.

mech-w12-q3.question: Placing a machine on its spring mounts compresses the mounts by 2.5 mm. What is the natural frequency of the system? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w12-q3.explanation: ωn = √(g/δst) = √(9.81/0.0025) = √3924 = 62.6 rad/s. fn = 62.6/(2π) = 9.97 Hz. 62.6 Hz comes from writing rad/s as Hz. 0.315 Hz and 1.98 Hz come from plugging in 2.5 without converting δst to metres.

mech-w12-q4.question: A system has m = 4 kg, k = 1600 N/m and damping coefficient c = 40 N·s/m. What is the damping ratio ζ?
mech-w12-q4.explanation: c_c = 2√(km) = 2√(1600 × 4) = 2 × 80 = 160 N·s/m. ζ = c/c_c = 40/160 = 0.25 (underdamped). 0.5 comes from dropping the 2 in c_c and using c/√(km) = 40/80. 0.025 is c/k (= 40/1600), which is not even dimensionless.

mech-w12-q5.question: In a damped free-vibration record, two successive peaks have amplitudes of 10 mm and 6 mm. What is the damping ratio ζ?
mech-w12-q5.explanation: δ = ln(10/6) = 0.511. ζ = δ/√(4π² + δ²) = 0.511/√(39.48 + 0.26) = 0.081 (for small ζ, δ/2π also gives ≈ 0.081). 0.511 is δ, not ζ. 0.40 comes from taking the fractional drop in amplitude (4/10) as ζ. 0.163 = δ/π, i.e. π instead of 2π.

mech-w12-q6.question: A system with m = 10 kg, k = 4000 N/m, c = 40 N·s/m is driven by a force F(t) = 20 sin(20t) N. What is the steady-state amplitude?
options: Infinite, because it is at resonance
mech-w12-q6.explanation: ωn = √(4000/10) = 20 rad/s = ω, so r = 1 (resonance). ζ = 40/(2√(4000 × 10)) = 40/400 = 0.1. X = (F₀/k)/(2ζ) = (20/4000)/0.2 = 0.025 m = 25 mm. 5 mm is just the static deflection F₀/k. An infinite amplitude needs zero damping — here ζ = 0.1 limits it to 5 times the static value. 50 mm comes from dividing by ζ instead of 2ζ.

mech-w12-q7.question: A 5 kg mass sits on a 2000 N/m spring (no damping). What is the natural circular frequency ωn?
mech-w12-q7.explanation: ωn = √(k/m) = √(2000/5) = √400 = 20 rad/s. 400 comes from forgetting the square root. 3.18 is the value of fn (in Hz) (20/2π), not ωn. 0.05 is the inverted formula √(m/k).

mech-w12-q8.question: Two springs, k₁ = 300 N/m and k₂ = 500 N/m, support a mass in parallel (both stretch together). What is the equivalent stiffness?
mech-w12-q8.explanation: In parallel both springs push at the same stretch, so k_eq = 300 + 500 = 800 N/m. 187.5 N/m is the series formula (300 × 500/800). 400 N/m is the average, and 200 N/m the difference — neither has a physical meaning here.

mech-w12-q9.question: If a damped system has damping ratio ζ = 1, what does its free vibration look like?
options: No oscillation, but a very slow return to rest
No oscillation, fastest return to rest
mech-w12-q9.explanation: ζ = 1 is critical damping: the system does not oscillate and returns to equilibrium in the shortest time. Oscillating while decaying is the ζ < 1 (underdamped) behaviour, and a slow return without oscillation is ζ > 1 (overdamped). In free damped vibration the amplitude never grows.

mech-w12-q10.question: A system has ωn = 30 rad/s and damping ratio ζ = 0.2. What is the damped natural frequency ωd?
mech-w12-q10.explanation: ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²) = 30√(1 − 0.04) = 30 × 0.980 = 29.4 rad/s. 24.0 rad/s comes from subtracting ζ instead of ζ² (30 × 0.8). 28.8 rad/s comes from forgetting the square root (30 × 0.96). 30.6 rad/s uses a plus — damping never raises the frequency.

mech-w12-q11.question: An 8 kg mass oscillates on a 3200 N/m spring (no damping). What is the period T of the oscillation?
mech-w12-q11.explanation: ωn = √(3200/8) = 20 rad/s. T = 2π/ωn = 0.314 s. 0.050 s is 1/ωn, forgetting the 2π. 3.18 s comes from writing the frequency fn (Hz) as the period. 0.157 s uses π instead of 2π.

mech-w12-q12.question: A system with m = 20 kg, k = 8000 N/m and ζ = 0.2 is driven by F(t) = 100 sin(30t) N. What is the steady-state amplitude?
mech-w12-q12.explanation: ωn = √(8000/20) = 20 rad/s, r = 30/20 = 1.5, r² = 2.25. F₀/k = 100/8000 = 12.5 mm. Denominator = √((1 − 2.25)² + (2 × 0.2 × 1.5)²) = √(1.5625 + 0.36) = 1.387. X = 12.5/1.387 = 9.02 mm. 12.5 mm is only the static deflection. 10.0 mm comes from ignoring the damping term (12.5/1.25). 5.56 mm comes from dropping the "1 −" and dividing by r² alone.

mech-w12-q13.question: In a damped vibration record the amplitude starts at 20 mm and falls to 5 mm after 4 cycles. What is the damping ratio ζ?
mech-w12-q13.explanation: For n cycles, δ = (1/n)·ln(x₀/xₙ) = ln(4)/4 = 0.347. ζ = δ/√(4π² + δ²) = 0.347/√(39.48 + 0.12) = 0.055. 0.221 comes from forgetting to divide by the 4 cycles (ln4/2π). 0.347 is δ, not ζ. 0.028 divides by 4π instead of 2π.

mech-w12-q14.question: A system with m = 5 kg, k = 5000 N/m and c = 50 N·s/m is driven by a harmonic force of amplitude 30 N exactly at its natural frequency. What is the steady-state amplitude?
mech-w12-q14.explanation: c_c = 2√(km) = 2√25000 = 316.2 N·s/m, so ζ = 50/316.2 = 0.158. At resonance (r = 1) X = F₀/(2ζk) = 30/(2 × 0.158 × 5000) = 0.0190 m = 19.0 mm. 6.0 mm is only the static deflection F₀/k. 37.9 mm comes from dividing by ζ instead of 2ζ. 0.95 mm comes from multiplying the static deflection by ζ.

mech-w12-q15.question: A machine on its spring mounts shows a 4 mm static deflection (negligible damping). For the force transmitted through the mounts to be less than F₀ (isolation), roughly what is the minimum operating speed of the machine? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
mech-w12-q15.explanation: ωn = √(g/δst) = √(9.81/0.004) = 49.5 rad/s. Isolation needs r > √2, so ω > 1.414 × 49.5 = 70.0 rad/s = 70.0 × 60/2π ≈ 669 rpm. 473 rpm is just the natural frequency (r = 1, i.e. resonance) — where the transmitted force is the largest. 70 rpm writes rad/s as rpm, and 946 rpm assumes r > 2.
